articles.title: Donald Trump says PH, US clinch 'big' trade deal
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced that the Philippines and the United States had secured a “big” trade deal as the two leaders held bilateral talks in Malacañang.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 2:53pm
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced that the Philippines and the United States had secured a “big” trade deal as the two leaders held bilateral talks in Malacañang.

“We've just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made by far, and it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with it,” Trump said during a state luncheon at Malacañang.
“I'm proud to say that we're making the alliance between the United States and the Philippines much stronger than it's ever been before, especially with the consummation of this deal,” he added.
Trump did not provide further details about the trade agreement.
Meanwhile, Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel “Babes” Romualdez said the deal involves food and energy supply.
“The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements,” he said.

In his remarks at the luncheon, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the Philippines and the United States continued to strengthen their partnership in trade, investment, energy, technology, resilience, supply chains and education, among other areas.

“I am confident that your visit will give fresh momentum to our partnership and open new opportunities for our two countries to work even more closely together for our peoples, for our region, for the peace and prosperity that we all seek,” Marcos said.
Trump is in the Philippines from Nov. 17 to 18. He arrived late Tuesday afternoon to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits.
His visit has drawn protests from various groups across the country, particularly over the proposed Pax Silica initiative.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Speaker calls on ASEAN lawmakers to pass laws to increase trade among members, address AI dangers
articles.summary: Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III on Wednesday called on Southeast Asian lawmakers to pass laws which will increase trade and other avenues of cooperation in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 2:32pm

Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III on Wednesday called on Southeast Asian lawmakers to pass laws which will increase trade and other avenues of cooperation in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), saying goods should freely flow in the 11-strong regional bloc.
Dy made the call during his keynote speech during the opening of the 47th General Assembly of the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly.

“Prosperity for all is the very purpose of ASEAN. And parliaments hold the tools to deliver it: laws that open markets fairly, budgets that build roads, ports, and schools, and oversight that ensures the benefits reach those who need them most,” Dy said.

“Growth should widen the circle. A rice farmer should receive a fair price for her harvest. A fisherman should be able to sell his catch in other towns. A small business in a provincial market should be able to reach customers in ten other countries. And a young graduate should be able to find work that makes full use of her talent,” Dy added.
Likewise, Dy said ASEAN lawmakers should stand together in fighting the challenges of artificial intelligence (AI) and regulating its benefits.

“Our farmers are already experiencing the digital transformation. Today, a farmer in the Mekong Delta checks the weather and the price of rice on her phone before deciding when to harvest. A young developer in Laos writes code for a company in Malaysia. A weaver in the Philippines sells her fabric to buyers in Indonesia. This is the ASEAN of 2045 arriving ahead of time. But the same networks also carry scams, disinformation, and threats to our privacy,” Dy said.

“Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone. Our parliaments must therefore learn from one another and move forward together: on cybersecurity, consumer protection, the responsible use of AI, and extending connectivity to the last village still waiting for it,” Dy added.

Ultimately, Dy said working together shared prosperity is anchored on the ASEAN’s Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia inked 50 years ago, a commitment that is much needed today as the ASEAN countries bear the brunt of high oil prices amid the war between the United States and Iran.

“Their promise was simple and brave: we will respect one another, we will settle our differences peacefully, and we will work together. Half a century later, that promise still holds. That commitment matters more than ever,” Dy said.

“This year, conflict far from our shores led to higher fuel prices, and families in every one of our countries felt the impact. Through every challenge, the spirit of the Treaty has been our anchor. As parliamentarians, we are the guardians. We keep it alive every time we pick up the phone to reach a counterpart across the border, every time we disagree in this hall and yet part as friends,” Dy added. —VAL, GMA News

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 2:28pm

United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday said America is expanding its defense cooperation with the Philippines amid its continuing moves to sell US weapons to its treaty partner in Southeast Asia.
Trump spoke on the matter as he and Philippine President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. held bilateral talks during the US president's state visit to the Philippines.
"Working with President Marcos, we're also expanding our defense cooperation, which has always been a key pillar of security for this part of the world," Trump said during his speech.
The US president also said that since he took office, he has approved arms sales to the Philippines of over $5 billion.
Trump also shared that the US is expanding its armaments factory with the construction of some 21 plants.
Asked about maritime tensions in the West Philippine Sea, Trump said, "I'm not concerned about that at all. That'll be taken care of."

Trump's response was also in line with a question asking about the United States' preparedness with regard to its Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) with the Philippines. The MDT, signed in 1951, commits the Philippines and the United States to come to each other's defense in the event of an armed attack on either country.

Trump's presence in the Philippines from November 17 to 18 has drawn protests from various groups, condemning his alleged role in soaring fuel prices due to the US-Israel war with Iran, as well as the US-led Pax Silica initiative. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: US Democrats flip Alaska Senate seat as Mary Peltola wins race
articles.summary: The US Senate's final outstanding midterm election race has been won by Mary Peltola. She unseats Republican Dan Sullivan after winning 50.1% of the vote.

image.caption: The so-called 'blue tsunami' that saw Democrats sweep to victory across the US has swept across AlaskaImage: Lindsey Wasson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Associated Press has declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner of Alaska's Senate race after making it just over the 50% mark on first-rank votes.
Alaska was the last outstanding Senate race to be declared in the US midterm elections 2026 and makes it the ninth Republican-held Senate seat to be flipped.
The latest victory means the Democrats now hold a 56-44 majority in the US Senate. The 53-year-old is the first Democratic senator from the state in almost 20 years.
Peltola promises to deliver for 'Alaska's working families'
"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said.
Peltola beat Republican Dan Sullivan's 131,844 with 144,302 votes, the victory coming after an update in the vote count pushed her to 50.1% of the votes.
Peltola will now become one of the first two Native American women to ever be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.
Alaska's vast geography, remote rural communities and lengthy absentee ballot process contributed to a protracted count, with the Senate race taking over two weeks to produce a winner.
Progress or not? Democrats, Republicans pick new leaders in Congress
Vote siphon allegations

The Alaskan Senate race garnered a high degree of national interest after a New York Times report that aides to Peltola allegedly tried to use a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, in an attempt to siphon votes from the Republican Dan Sullivan.
The Trump administration had approached the courts to block certifying the results in the event of there being a potential mix-up.
The legal bid was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.
"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.
Peltola has denied any knowledge of an alleged plot. In any case, the margin of victory was greater than the number of votes won by the challenger Dan Sullivan, at just 4, 760.

The Democrats' majority had already been secured, allowing them to block legislation and begin investigations into members of President Donald Trump's administration, but the Alaska win will likely also have a morale impact on both sides.

articles.title: ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio
articles.summary:
The US secretary of state was speaking after Microsoft, major banks, and the National Security Agency were all affected by technical failures in recent days

US secretary of state Marco Rubio…

blocks.text: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the cascade of service outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or to a malign actor.

In recent days, Microsoft, major US banks, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Donald Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike demand the White House answer for the disruptions.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.

He made the comments as he travelled with Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday, before flying to the tech hub of Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.

Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the outages on Tuesday. “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila.

The series of outages began on Thursday, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down, paralysing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to “an earlier network capacity upgrade”.
Flights across the US were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since the September 11 attacks. The US Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.

By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JP Morgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related”.
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
Then on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance”.
Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, said the White House needed to do more to explain the situation.

“What I would say to the White House is: transparency is key,” Leavitt said on Fox News. Later, she praised the White House for having director of national intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network.

“Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber-attack incident,” Clayton said, explaining that the US government believes the incidents were caused by security upgrades that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.

Democrat Mark Warner, the chair of the Senate intelligence committee reiterated that message, saying “there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.

“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change.
“The evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

articles.title: [In This Economy] Notes from Cambodia
articles.summary: Even Cambodia is faring a bit better than the Philippines, and the data show that plainly

blocks.text: As all eyes were on Manila for the Philippines’ hosting of the ASEAN Summit, I got to explore Cambodia again for the first time in almost a decade.
My jaw positively dropped when I went through Phnom Penh’s new airport.
Techo International Airport opened in September 2025. Its terminal is huge, with a roof inspired by Cambodia’s national flower and a ceiling patterned after traditional Khmer fishing equipment.
Immediately I thought about how lamentable the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) is by comparison.

Sure, there are questions about how Techo was built. A Chinese state-owned company built the passenger terminal, and the first phase alone cost a whopping US$2.3 billion. Critics assail how the contracts were awarded and who will end up bearing the financial risks.
At any rate, it cannot be denied that Techo is a first-class airport. If the main international gateway of a country is any indication, I’m sad to report that Cambodia beat us in this aspect.

I would even venture to say Cambodians are much more ready to receive guests for the annual ASEAN Summit than we are. (In the past few days, they actually received delegates for the Francophonie Summit, which they are hosting for the first time ever.)

blocks.caption: FLOWER PATTERN. The author at the new Techo International Airport, about 40 minutes away from central Phnom Penh.

blocks.text: An airport, of course, signals only so much, and it can’t hide the fact that in 2026 Cambodia is in dire straits like us.

For this year, the World Bank expects Cambodia’s economy to grow by just 3.5%, down from an estimated 5.3% in 2025. Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects growth of just 3%, with inflation averaging 5.6%. Expensive energy and weaker tourism are among the reasons for the slowdown.

Sounds familiar? In my last column, I argued that the Philippines had entered stagflation territory. We’d had two quarters in a row of unusually weak growth and high inflation, even after I changed how I accounted for the pandemic in my growth benchmark.
Still, Cambodia is faring a bit better than us, and the data show that plainly.
What also stood out to me was how much foreign direct investment (FDI) Cambodia already gets. In 2025, it took in $5.1 billion or about a tenth of its gross domestic product.

Foreign investment is also spreading beyond garments to areas like electronics and renewable energy. But the IMF says Cambodia needs to attract higher-quality investment and spur more investment by Cambodian firms.
Cambodia teaches us that foreign investments are necessary but not sufficient for sustained growth. A lot of work remains after foreign money comes in.

For instance, a foreign factory can hire a lot of workers and export a lot of goods while buying its sophisticated inputs overseas and keeping its engineering work at headquarters. The gains get bigger when local suppliers can win contracts and local engineers get to solve problems they used to send back to headquarters.

That brings me back to Pax Silica, discussions of which heated up in the past couple of days in the run-up to our ASEAN hosting. Hundreds of protesters were arrested, bringing back images of how protests were stifled by the old Marcos regime.

We don’t know quite yet how much money will come into New Clark City. But it’s important to ask: What will Filipino engineers actually get to do there? Will they run the tests or develop them, too? Will Philippine firms have a shot at supplying the factory? And if we’re offering tax breaks or paying for infrastructure, what commitments are we getting in return?
Many questions linger in the air as the Pax Silica framework is set to be formalized by December, after the ASEAN Summit and the quick visit of US President Donald Trump.

blocks.caption: Sorry, Marcos can’t keep his ‘very, very important guest’ waiting

blocks.text: I also learned that Cambodia has spearheaded reforms in public financial management or PFM. It refers to how the government plans, spends, and accounts for public money.
This fact I picked up from the 21st International Convention of the East Asian Economic Association held in Siem Reap on November 14 and 15.

In a session on the Cambodian economy, I learned that public financial management has been the subject of a sustained reform program there since 2004. (The finance ministry’s own reform steering committee helped host the conference.)
Think about that for a moment. They’ve been at it for more than 20 years.

To be fair, the Philippines has its own PFM roadmap for 2024 to 2028. But the reforms need to level up well after 2028, in the wake of the flood control scandal of 2025 and the emerging scandal concerning the 2027 pre-election budget.

Take the multipurpose buildings, farm-to-market roads, and flood control projects that keep mushrooming in the national budget. Before any is funded, an agency should be able to tell us where it’s going, whom it will serve, and why it deserves priority.

Then when Congress adds any project, we should be able to see who asked for it and what appraisal it went through. When the money gets disbursed, people should be able to check whether the road was actually built.

Lawmakers have boasted of “reforms” like livestreamed budget deliberations and new online portals that supposedly enable ordinary Filipinos to scrutinize the budget. But in truth, many of these are perfunctory reforms that do nothing to fix the entrenched culture of patronage-driven budgeting.
Bad budgeting drags growth, and if we fail to take PFM seriously, then Cambodia might beat us here, too.
Finally, right before my flight back to Manila, I managed to squeeze in a quick visit to S-21, now the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum in Phnom Penh.

If you don’t have any idea about it, the Khmer Rouge took an ordinary school and turned it into a prison and torture center back in the mid-1970s. The rooms are still there, and so are the photographs and records of the people they imprisoned.
I had goosebumps the whole time. Even after I left the museum, I was still shaken.

Even in broad daylight, I was horrified by the idea that humans can do such despicable things to fellow humans. S-21 was a factory of torture and death, and visiting the museum is not for the faint-hearted.

It made me think about what we’ve done to preserve the memory of martial law under Ferdinand Marcos Sr. Sure, we’ve had a law since 2013 that calls for a memorial, museum, and library for victims of human rights violations.

blocks.caption: DELAYED. Scale model of the Freedom Memorial Museum. Courtesy of UP Diliman Information Office

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the University of the Philippines and the Human Rights Violations Victims’ Memorial Commission have committed to building the Freedom Memorial Museum in UP Diliman. It was supposed to have been opened in 2022, on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the martial law declaration. But four years on, as one would expect under yet another Marcos presidency, no progress has been made.

In Phnom Penh, locals and tourists alike can visit the gruesome Tuol Sleng museum as a ghastly reminder of their past. At the end of the tour, in the central courtyard, one can pay respects to the victims of the genocide at a six-meter, non-denominational stone stupa that rises above black marble plaques. Engraved are the names of 12,272 documented S-21 prisoners.

blocks.caption: NEVER FORGET. A marker at the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum: “Never will we forget the crimes committed during the Democratic Kampuchea regime.” Photo by JC Punongbayan

blocks.text: Similarly, we need to have a stronger reckoning and memorialization of the victims of Martial Law. We have the Bantayog ng mga Bayani, sure, but it needs a lot more financial support, and the museum at UP must finally be opened after long delays.

Apart from the martial law victims, we need to seriously memorialize as well the thousands who died under the bloody war on drugs by former president Rodrigo Duterte, who will soon stand trial at the International Criminal Court.
At least 1.7 million people died under the Khmer Rouge. The UN-backed tribunal convicted just three men, including the person who ran S-21.
I just hope the families of those killed in Duterte’s drug war see justice, too. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

articles.title: Fact check: Viral 'Duterte ASEAN vs. BBM ASEAN' post recycles 2019 SEA Games footage
articles.summary: A viral Duterte vs BBM ASEAN hosting comparison has one problem: The footage is from 2019

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 2:21pm
Former President Rodrigo Duterte and President Bongbong Marcos.
PCO

MANILA, Philippines — A viral social media post framing a comparison between former President Rodrigo Duterte’s and President Bongbong Marcos’ hosting of the ASEAN summit recycles footage from the 2019 Southeast Asian Games.
The viral Threads post falsely presents 2019 SEA Games footage as Duterte’s ASEAN Summit hosting.
Screenshot taken Nov. 18, 2026, 1:30 p.m.

In a Threads post on November 17, a compilation of clips was presented as footage of the former administration’s hosting of ASEAN leaders under Duterte’s “legacy,” and used to criticize Marcos’ chairship.
The video also features the text “PRRD with 7b budget” and “Duterte ASEAN vs BBM ASEAN.”
The post’s caption said:
"THE PEOPLE REMEMBER. HISTORY DOESN'T LIE. AND NO AMOUNT OF PROPAGANDA CAN CHANGE THAT." ???? Strong, direct, and unapologetic. #DUTERTELEGACY #PROUDFILIPINO
Rating: This is false.
Facts
Every clip included in the post was taken from the 2019 SEA Games opening ceremony, misrepresented as footage from the 2017 ASEAN Summit hosted by the Philippines under Duterte.
The Threads post’s compilation of clips was taken from a 2024 TikTok reel posted by a pro-Duterte account praising the former president's leadership.
The SEAG Network uploaded footage of the 2019 SEA Games opening ceremony at the Philippine Arena on November 30, 2019.
The footage used was sourced from the opening ceremony of the 2019 SEA Games held at the Philippine Arena, uploaded by the SEAG Network on YouTube on November 30, 2019.
The Duterte administration allocated P15.5 billion for the Philippines’ hosting of the ASEAN summit and related activities in 2017, not P7 billion as claimed in the video.
In comparison, the Marcos administration allocated a P22.9-billion budget for the 2026 ASEAN Summit hosted by the country.
Why we fact-checked this
The Philippines turned over the ASEAN chairship to Singapore on November 17, the final day of the bloc's 49th Summit.
Criticism over the P22.9-billion allocation for the 2026 ASEAN chairship prompted Malacañang to clarify that the amount also covers the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu in May 2026.
Preparations for the November summit included major infrastructure and venue preparations at the Philippine International Convention Center and World Trade Center in Pasay City.
As of November 18, the Threads post has garnered more than 2,000 likes and 100 reposts.

articles.summary: Climate campaigners say the AI pledge would only work if the US hyperscalers signed up and if it were mandatory

blocks.text: PROTEST. Activists and locals attend the People’s Climate March as part of a global day of action, “demanding climate justice, an end to fossil fuels and a just transition that puts people and the planet before corporate profit”, where the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) is also taking place, in Antalya, Turkey, on November 14, 2026.
Umit Bektas/Reuters
Climate campaigners say the AI pledge would only work if the US hyperscalers signed up and if it were mandatory

items: China's Alibaba is the only major tech company to sign the UN-backed Antalya AI Pledge aimed at reducing the environmental impact of artificial intelligence, while major US companies have not participated.

The pledge encourages governments and companies to use cleaner energy for AI, improve infrastructure efficiency, track emissions, and enhance AI access in developing countries, attracting 90 endorsements including nine countries.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ANTALYA, Turkey – China’s Alibaba is the only big tech company so far to have signed a UN-backed promise to reduce the environmental impact of artificial intelligence, as major US companies have stayed away.

The Antalya AI Pledge, launched on Monday, November 16, by Turkey, the host of COP31 climate talks until the end of this week, calls on governments and companies to take voluntary measures to power AI with cleaner energy.
Signatories are also urged to support more efficient infrastructure, track emissions, and improve access to AI in developing countries.

Publicized for weeks in advance of the summit on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, the promise attracted 90 endorsements at its launch, including just nine countries and Chinese e-commerce and technology conglomerate Alibaba. Private companies, think tanks and nongovernmental organizations were also among those to back the pledge.
Meta, Microsoft, and Google, which operate global data-center networks, AI, and internet infrastructure at enormous scale, and chipmaker Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

Amazon declined to comment on the pledge, but said it had a new target to reduce the carbon intensity of its electricity consumption by 65% by 2030 from a 2019 baseline and reiterated its commitment to net-zero carbon emissions by 2040.
A report released on Monday found the United States’ more than 400 hyperscale data centers emit roughly as much carbon dioxide as Denmark.
South Korea, a significant user of AI, was among the countries that signed, but the other government signatories represented small countries.

The United States has stayed away from the UN climate talks for a second year in succession after President Donald Trump withdrew from the UN climate process. Trump has championed both untrammeled expansion of AI and the continued use of fossil fuel.
But companies such as Amazon also face a different pressure from some shareholders concerned about the growing environmental impact and social opposition to the data centers their business requires.

The UN’s technology agency, the International Telecommunication Union, said it is engaging with major tech companies as part of its outreach effort, and would keep the pledge open to signatures until the next UN climate talks, COP32, at the end of next year.
Tech firms had been among the most visible corporate participants at previous UN climate summits, promoting goals, including carbon-negative operations and net-zero emissions.
But the rapid expansion of AI and data centers has complicated those ambitions.
While still investing in renewable energy, some of the companies have supported new natural gas generation.
Climate campaigners said the AI pledge would only work if the US hyperscalers signed up and if it were mandatory.
“Voluntary standards alone are not enough,” Julie Cerqueira, chief program officer at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Thomas Markle Sr. faces child sex abuse raps --PNP
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police on Wednesday said it has filed criminal charges against Thomas Markle Sr. for alleged child sex abuse.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 2:11pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Wednesday said it has filed criminal charges against Thomas Markle Sr. for alleged child sex abuse.

In a statement, PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said the raps are for violations of the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation (OSAEC) and Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials (CSAEM) Act.
These charges involve the distribution and possession of child sexual abuse or exploitation materials (CSAEM).
The Women and Children Protection Center (WCPC) - Visayas Field Unit filed the complaints before the Prosecutor’s Office on Monday.
Co said the complaints would undergo evaluation and case build-up.
Meanwhile, digital forensic examination of the remaining digital devices seized in connection with the investigation is still ongoing.
"Additional evidence may be submitted in support of the criminal complaints already filed or may be utilized for filing of additional criminal complaints, if warranted," Co said.
Markle, 82, is the biological father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex.
He had stayed in the Philippines for approximately nine to 10 months, beginning in 2025.
Authorities recovered around 7,500 photographs and one video showing underage boys and girls of Asian, Latina, and European descent from devices linked to Markle Sr.
Some of the minors in the recovered materials appeared to be Filipino.
On November 6, Markle was arrested in Florida, United States on a charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Xi, Putin blast Western 'protectionism,' sanctions before meeting Trump at APEC
articles.summary: SHENZHEN, China -- China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions as the two set…

blocks.text: SHENZHEN, China — China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions as the two set the stage for a high-stakes trilateral meeting with Donald Trump.

They delivered their speeches at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, ahead of US President Trump's arrival from Manila, where he was meeting key regional allies.

The three men are due to meet on the sidelines on Thursday and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.

The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
It has also unnerved leaders of smaller economies, particularly in Europe and Asia, who fear the world's greatest military powers will disregard their interests.

In his opening address, Xi urged support for what he called "free and open trade," trying to portray his country as a stable partner on the global stage, in contrast with main economic rival the US, which has raised tariffs and adopted a more muscular foreign policy under Trump.
Message resonates with global south

Xi's remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, which could further complicate a fragile trade truce with Beijing. China has pledged to retaliate.

"We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains," Xi told an audience of business executives.
Western trade partners have criticized China for running annual trade surpluses in excess of $1 trillion through policies that support its manufacturing sector at the expense of its consumers.

Beijing says its growth model is appropriate for an economy still catching up with the world's richest, but Washington, Brussels and others are concerned about China's supply chain dominance providing the country with geopolitical leverage and say its policies threaten their industries and jobs.

Xi said China will continue to invest in its industrial complex and develop new technologies that would also benefit other countries. The world's second-largest economy will lower tariffs and further open up its markets, while standing up against protectionism and unilateralism, he added.

His "message is likely to resonate with many Global South countries and reinforces Beijing's effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group.
Trump's trip to Asia is his first since his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections, while allegations involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy add to the tension.

Still, most analysts expect Washington and Beijing to keep ties relatively stable as Trump and Xi are set to follow their Thursday meeting in Shenzhen with their fourth of the year at the Group of 20 gathering in Miami in December.
High-stakes meeting

Putin, who was speaking after Ukraine destroyed the vital Kerch road bridge linking Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war, followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as "former hegemons."
He said Europe was in a "humiliating decline" and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired, instead making his country stronger.
"Experience has shown that the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having lost much of their intimidating power," Putin said.
"While sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth—let alone crushing the economies of competitors."

The Kremlin this week dismissed comparisons with the Yalta Conference as "games of political scientists," but said the meeting will have a major impact on global affairs. Beijing said the trilateral is of "groundbreaking significance" and will promote world peace.
Trump also floated the possibility that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but that has not been confirmed.
On Tuesday, Taiwan and Japan flagged incursions by Russian aircraft into their airspace.

Putin described the world as "turbulent" and "marked by a fragmenting global economy and rising military-political risks," but said disagreements between countries can be addressed by "sitting at the table."
"I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States," he said. — Reuters

Carlos Barria/Reuters

'Just think of it as providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do, that you have done, and continue to do, and that is in front of you,' Marcos tells Trump at their bilateral meeting in Manila

items: After a long workday, many people, including President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., appreciate comfort food, with Jollibee representing Filipino identity, especially abroad.
During a bilateral meeting with US President Donald Trump, Marcos highlighted Jollibee's popularity and had snacks delivered to provide Trump with a taste of Manila.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

After a long and hard day at work, many people look forward to a good meal, preferably comfort food. In the Philippines, that arguably equates to home-grown Jollibee, which has become synonymous to Filipino identity, especially abroad.
That was apparently the train of thought of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. when United States President Donald Trump was in town for a brief state visit.

In his opening remarks during his bilateral meeting with Trump on Wednesday, November 18, Marcos acknowledged the US leader’s tight schedule in the Philippines. Trump arrived late Tuesday afternoon, November 17, and headed straight to the Philippine International Convention Center to attend the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue meeting, the ASEAN-US Special Summit, and other meetings after the conclusion of the 49th ASEAN Summit.
“Your schedule has been packed to the hilt, which is not exactly a surprise because we know how hard you work,” Marcos told Trump.
The Philippine leader said this was why he decided to at least give Trump and his delegation a “taste of Manila” and had Jollibee snacks delivered to them.

“Jollibee is a very very popular chain, and one of their main products is fried chicken, and we are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity,” Marcos said.
Trump responded, “Oh wow, that’s interesting.”

“You have been working very hard, Mr. President….So just think of it as providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do, that you have done, and continue to do, and that is in front of you,” Marcos said.
Diplomacy via Jollibee is nothing new. In July, Marcos and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney paid a visit to a Jollibee store in Vancouver following their bilateral meeting.

blocks.caption: Hindi Ito Marites: Diplomacy via Jollibee

blocks.text: The company is operating over 100 stores in North America and plans to reach 500 stores by 2030. (READ: How Jollibee became Filipino food’s biggest ambassador in the US)

In the recently concluded 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and Related Summits, the Jollibee mascot, wearing a barong, made an appearance at the International Media Center, located at the World Trade Center in Pasay City on Tuesday.
That’s days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese sampled Chickenjoy and announced that the food chain will also open its doors across New South Wales and Victoria.

“Its establishment in Australia will answer the diaspora’s calls to make home-style Filipino dishes more accessible and provide an opportunity for Australians to experience Filipino cuisine and culture firsthand,” according to a news release from Albanese’s website.
As for the late night Jollibee delivery to Trump, well, it just showed how Marcos cared for his “very, very important guest.” Bida ang saya nga naman! – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records
articles.summary:
Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service

The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of…

blocks.text: The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years.

Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added.

The figures likely underestimate the scale of the abuse. Only those cases where the NHS had confirmed that staff had wrongly accessed patients’ notes or medical histories were included, and nearly half of trusts failed to provide precise data.

The disclosure follows a recent series of high-profile cases. Last month it emerged that 15 NHS staff had been sacked after accessing records belonging to victims of the 2023 Nottingham attack, in which Valdo Calocane killed two 19-year-old students, Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, and attempted to kill three other people.
Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust (NUH) said in October that it had so far dismissed 15 staff, issued 15 final written warnings and two first written warnings.

In May, it emerged that dozens of staff at University Hospitals of Liverpool Group had looked at the records of victims of the 2024 Southport attack, which left three girls dead and 10 others injured.
The records of a three-year-old boy hurt after falling into a crocodile pit in Cambridgeshire in June were also viewed by about 40 hospital staff.
Figures obtained under freedom of information laws by the Press Association show there were 3,029 incidents of staff inappropriately accessing patient records between 2021-22 and 2025-26.
But the true extent of the problem is likely to be much higher. Only 79 of 143 acute hospital and ambulance trusts in England provided precise figures.

Trusts must report breaches posing a risk to patients’ rights to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) within 72 hours. The regulator’s chief executive, Paul Arnold, has written to health leaders demanding a crackdown on the snoopers.
“When we seek medical care, we trust the NHS with some of our most sensitive information and we need to be confident that only people with a legitimate reason will ever access our records.

“Looking at medical records out of curiosity is unacceptable and jeopardises the vital trust people place in the health service. These figures are deeply concerning and I know how much distress this type of behaviour causes patients and families.”
Rachel Power, chief executive at the Patients Association, said the incidents eroded trust in the wider NHS, and a further lack of transparency “deepens that damage”.

“Patients need confidence that strong safeguards are in place, that inappropriate access will be detected and acted on without delay, and that they will be the first to know, not the last, when their confidentiality has been breached.”
In September, the head of NHS England, Jim Mackey, said staff suspected of snooping on patients’ medical records should be suspended immediately and barred from using health service computers.
Earlier that month, the Health Service Journal reported that 214 NHS staff had been sacked, three suspended and 540 given final written warnings for snooping on patients’ records since 2020.

One employee was dismissed after viewing up to 179 people’s records, another had accessed their spouse’s details in a “potential domestic violence situation”, and others had shared information they had gathered in WhatsApp groups.

articles.title: How to deal with a class difference in friendships? Make fun of your privileged friends
articles.summary:
Lasting cross-class friendships involve routinely ‘taking the piss’ out of the more privileged party, research by the LSE shows

Routinely “taking the piss” out of more privileged friends is…
articles.byline: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent

blocks.text: Routinely “taking the piss” out of more privileged friends is one of the main ways people cope with a class difference in their friendships, research has found.
Cross-class friendships are widespread and mutually beneficial, a study by the London School of Economics showed, but a class gap can still pose an “omnipresent threat” to friendships.

More privileged friends often provide financial support or cultural guidance to less privileged friends navigating elite spaces, the research found, and in return get a better understanding of the world outside their immediate sphere.
But because the more tangible support tends to flow one way, it often brings about feelings of inequality or indebtedness, said the sociologist Prof Sam Friedman, who co-wrote the research.

In some cases, it becomes a source of tension or sends friendships into a downward spiral, said Friedman, the author of The Class Ceiling and Born To Rule, which explored how the British elite has changed over the last 120 years.

He and Prof Rose Butler, from Deakin University in Australia, looked at successful and failed cross-class friendships and found that those that lasted exhibited “class diplomacy”. This involved making jokes, prioritising friendship over class differences and building empathy through talking about class differences.

A working-class man referred to as Peter in the study described making jokes about his friend, Julian. “It would be your typical private school boy jokes … and stuff like, I don’t know, about mummy and daddy’s credit card on a night out,” he said.

A working-class friend in a similar friendship said his more privileged friend’s reaction to these kinds of jokes made him respect him. He said: “I think the humour’s really important because essentially … he was quite thick [skinned], he never like got pissy or anything. A lot of the time he would take it on the chin.”

The paper’s starting point was two studies by economists in the US and UK that analysed billions of friendship ties on Facebook and said that cross-class friendships were a good thing because they gave working-class people social capital that propelled them towards upward social mobility, Friedman said.
He and Butler tested this claim using 42 in-depth interviews and found that humour was often pivotal to defusing tension.

One friend from a background self-described as “upper middle class” and “elitey”, said: “The having a laugh thing is such a big deal … like the therapeutic way of managing [the class difference] … He’ll take the piss out of me but it’s fine.”

Other more privileged friends would make jokes at their own expense. One working-class person in the study said about her friend from a wealthy background: “Every time I discovered a new house [that her family owned] I’d be like ‘Jesus Christ’ and would just let it slip, but both Sophie and me take the piss out of it. Like she’ll rip herself apart … she always does it before I can.”
Friedman said the humour in successful friendships never resorted to “punching down”. “It’s punching up that works,” he said.
Some friends coped with the difference by not discussing class. Less privileged friends talked about not wanting to call out snobbery.
after newsletter promotion

One middle-class person said about their less privileged friend: “I don’t think we really ever mention class. But I think we’re hyper aware of the difference. It feels like it’s conferred such real-life advantages and disadvantages that it almost is so difficult to speak about.”

Another friend from a less privileged background said: “I think he had a lot of learning to do and I think when both of us started to get to know one another, both his side realising how unbelievably lucky he’s had it, but on the flip me not being such a judgmental prick … it went both ways.”
Friedman also identified that “the emotional burden of confronting class difference often fell disproportionately on friends from less advantaged backgrounds”.

“This was partly due to the fact that most of these friendships had emerged in middle-class spaces where middle-class norms were dominant and often taken for granted,” according to the paper, published in the journal Social Forces on Wednesday.

“Such inequality was best encapsulated by the idiom ‘a chip on the shoulder’ – the idea that someone is habitually (and unreasonably) bitter because they feel they’ve been treated unfairly – and is normally deployed on the basis of social class in Britain.”
Friedman said working-class interviewees often described this phrase being used against them by their friends at some point, “or feared that it might be used against them”.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Claire Castro not appointed SC justice
articles.summary: Castro remains with the Presidential Communications Office and has denied applying for the position of Supreme Court associate justice

blocks.text: Claim: Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Undersecretary Claire Castro has been appointed as a Supreme Court (SC) associate justice.
Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube channel named “PINAS BALITA TV,” which has over 176,000 subscribers, posted the claim on November 4.
The video is titled, “Hala! Grabe ito! May bagong ma-appoint as Supreme Court Justice? Ante Kler lang ang sakalam dito!”
(This is intense! Someone new is being appointed as Supreme Court justice? Auntie Claire is the only strong one here!)

The video’s thumbnail shows an image of the Palace press officer wearing a judicial robe with other SC justices in the background. Text on the thumbnail claims she has been appointed and promoted to the high bench.
Another video, posted on October 28, bears a thumbnail image of Castro wearing a judicial robe with the text, “USec Claire sa Supreme Court?”
Several social media users expressed surprise at the supposed appointment, with some questioning her credentials.
As of writing, the November 4 video has garnered over 5,300 views and 284 likes.

The facts: Castro continues to serve as Palace press officer and PCO undersecretary. In fact, she has held several press briefings after the misleading video was posted, with the most recent one held on November 15.

While Castro is a lawyer, she explicitly denied applying for a judicial post when asked to comment on reports about her supposed appointment as SC associate justice. In a media briefing on October 27, Castro addressed speculation that she might be appointed to the High Court following reports that then-associate justice Rodil Zalameda was a top contender for the chief justice post, potentially opening up a vacancy for associate justice.
“Associate justice ng Supreme Court si ‘Ante Kler’? Hindi ako nag-apply. So, wala pong katotohanan ‘yun.” she said.
(‘Ante Kler’ as an associate justice of the Supreme Court? I didn’t apply. So, that’s not true.)
She added that she would not preempt President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in choosing the next chief justice.
On November 6, Marcos appointed Zalameda as the 28th chief justice of the country. He succeeds former Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who retired upon reaching the mandatory retirement age of 70.
Constitutional qualifications and process: Under Article VIII, Section 7 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, a candidate for the Supreme Court must meet the following qualifications:

items: Must be a natural-born citizen of the Philippines
Must be at least 40 years of age
Must have been a judge of a lower court or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines for at least 15 years

blocks.text: Moreover, under Article VIII, Sections 8 and 9 of the Constitution, the President can only appoint members of the Supreme Court from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for every vacancy.

Because Castro did not apply for the position, she was not on the JBC shortlist and could not have been legally considered or appointed to the High Court.Unrelated video content: The video itself does not provide any proof of Castro’s supposed appointment.

Instead, it features the narrator reacting to a news site’s social media posts involving Castro and Vice President Sara Duterte. He enumerates the qualifications required to become a Supreme Court justice and claims to assess whether Castro is eligible, yet fails to present any evidence that she was allegedly nominated or appointed.
Debunked: Rappler has debunked other false claims involving Castro:

items: FACT CHECK: Claire Castro not removed from her post, remains Palace press officer
FACT CHECK: Claire Castro quote blaming heavy floods on blocked drains is fake
FACT CHECK: Claire Castro quote on Marcos’ plans to run for VP is fake

blocks.text: Rappler has also fact-checked false claims originating from the same YouTube channel:

items: FACT CHECK: Lacson remains a senator, did not resign
FACT CHECK: No reports of SC order ousting Marcos
FACT CHECK: No report of Indonesian President confronting, scolding Marcos

blocks.text: – Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com
Lyndee Buenagua is a Metro Manila-based journalist who primarily covers Bicol and Baguio. She is also an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Marcos: PH, US explore ties in technology, superintelligence
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday said the Philippines and the United States are looking into a partnership in technology and superintelligence.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 1:39pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday said the Philippines and the United States are looking into a partnership in technology and superintelligence.

"Now we are also exploring new areas of cooperation, particularly in technology, where American leadership and innovation continue to lead the way," Marcos said in his speech during the bilateral meeting with US President Donald Trump.
"We also see tremendous opportunities to work more closely through American leadership in superintelligence," he added.
Marcos also expressed confidence that the Philippines and the US will find new and important ways to deepen partnerships.
Meanwhile, Trump described Marcos as his "fantastic" and "great" friend.

"We've known each other for a long time. And I very much appreciate your welcoming me and us back to the Philippines as we reaffirm one of America's oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific," Trump said in his speech.

"With this visit, we're building on these ties to make our partnership even closer, although I don't imagine it can get much closer because of the relationship that we've had for a long time," he added.
Meanwhile, Marcos shared that he ordered his staff to deliver a meal from Jollibee, the country's famous homegrown fast-food chain, to Trump and his delegation "to give a taste of Manila."
Trump arrived at Malacañang on Wednesday as part of his state visit to the Philippines.
He is in the Philippines from November 17-18.

Marking its 80 years of partnership in business, diplomacy, and people-to-people ties, the Philippines and the US launched a new edition of a booklet highlighting the countries' longstanding relationship.

The second edition of the booklet, “The Philippines Matters for America, America Matters for the Philippines,” commemorates eight decades of diplomatic relations between the two countries. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Successful’ ASEAN Summit ends with Marcos unable to solve its hardest problems
articles.summary: ‘I would say that it was a success simply because of the work that we were able to achieve,’ President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. says, despite no big breakthroughs on Myanmar or the long-awaited South…

blocks.text: HOST. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. waits for his fellow Southeast Asian leaders during the 49th ASEAN Summit retreat session in Pasay City on November 15, 2026.
Aaron Favila/Pool via Reuters

‘I would say that it was a success simply because of the work that we were able to achieve,’ President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. says, despite no big breakthroughs on Myanmar or the long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct

items: The 49th ASEAN Summit resulted in over a hundred outcome documents but failed to resolve ongoing issues such as the civil war in Myanmar and the South China Sea Code of Conduct negotiations.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared the summit a success, highlighting milestones like the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement and advancements in maritime cooperation.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – After three days of summits and a seemingly endless procession of meetings, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) had over a hundred outcome documents to show for its time in Manila.
Yet it also had a civil war in Myanmar with no end in sight and a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) that, despite two decades of negotiations, its members and China still could not agree on.
Such was the record of the Philippines’ ASEAN chairmanship, which President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared a “success” on Tuesday, November 17, as he formally handed over the reins to Singapore.

“I would say that it was a success simply because of the work that we were able to achieve. The one thing I did not want to do was to waste an opportunity such as this by just doing this hosting,” Marcos told the media following the summit’s closing ceremony.

The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits brought leaders to the Philippines in a world beset by overlapping crises. Ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine have thrown global energy and food supplies into disarray, El Niño threatens agricultural production, and economies across the region are reeling from rising costs and varying levels of domestic unrest. (READ: Marcos gov’t on track to miss growth target for fourth straight year)

Against this backdrop, Southeast Asian leaders and their allies had much to discuss across the different meetings that Manila has played host to. Read Rappler’s live updates for more details on the key developments.

To be fair, there were milestones. ASEAN signed its Digital Economy Framework Agreement, establishing common rules for digital trade and payments. All 11 members also signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding on the ASEAN Power Grid, with Marcos announcing that a proposed undersea cable would connect Sabah to Mindanao. The bloc also advanced initiatives on maritime cooperation, disaster response, online scams, and child protection.
But what of ASEAN’s most difficult problems?

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: PH ends ASEAN chairship with gains, but Myanmar and COC unresolved

blocks.text: Top on Marcos’ plate was Myanmar, still embroiled in a political crisis that has seen it sidelined from ASEAN since the military-backed government seized power in 2021.
Marcos said Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, serving as ASEAN’s special envoy, had focused on facilitating dialogue and expanding humanitarian assistance.
“None of those items are easy. However, the one that is easily understandable and immediately implementable is the assistance on the humanitarian side,” Marcos told the media on Tuesday.

ASEAN leaders agreed to pursue a “calibrated, progress-based approach” toward Myanmar, leaving open the possibility of gradually restoring its full political representation if the country demonstrates concrete progress under ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus. In their review of the Myanmar situation, the leaders also reiterated their “deep concern over the insufficient progress in the implementation of the 5PC.”
But until progress towards peace comes, Myanmar remains barred from having its political leaders join the high-stakes ASEAN summits and foreign ministers’ meetings.
“The ball is very much now in the court of Myanmar and its present leadership,” Marcos said.

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: Trump meets ASEAN leaders at special summit

blocks.text: It would also have been a perfect win to conclude COC negotiations during Marcos’ year at the helm of ASEAN. Instead, that too failed to live up to ambitions.
The President told reporters that 85% to 90% of the agreement had been completed — a more optimistic assessment than his foreign secretary’s earlier estimate of around 80%.
According to Marcos, much of the remaining work revolves around the definition of terms.

“There are definitions, there are phrases, and there are paragraphs that need to be clearly defined so that it is very understandable and very clear to everyone involved that these are the rules,” he said.

But absent from his remarks was perhaps the most contentious issue of all: whether the eventual COC would be legally binding. This is particularly important for the Philippines, given its continuing confrontations with China in the West Philippine Sea.

In the meantime, Marcos said ASEAN and China had reached a “tacit agreement” to continue abiding by the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea, the earlier, nonbinding framework that the COC is meant to build upon.

blocks.caption: Sorry, Marcos can’t keep his ‘very, very important guest’ waiting

blocks.text: Although the ASEAN closing ceremony was already over, leaders were asked to stretch their stay a little longer for one final meeting, a special summit with visiting US President Donald Trump.

Perhaps that was why Marcos was also mum on the controversial US-led Pax Silica initiative, which has drawn protests across the metro and in the provinces. Officials had already previously said no major announcement on the initiative was planned during the summit.
Unfortunately, there was little opportunity to press the Philippine leader further.
His final briefing allowed questions from just one pre-selected reporter before he was whisked away to meet a particularly important guest. Marcos, it seemed, had kept that guest waiting long enough.
“I can’t keep the president of the United States waiting, so I have to go. I’m sorry,” he told reporters on his way out.
And with that, Marcos was off to meet Trump, leaving Singapore, ASEAN’s 2027 chair, to inherit some very old problems to deal with. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Palace: Keeping streets clean post-ASEAN not government's job alone
articles.summary: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro urged Filipinos to practice proper trash disposal and help maintain cleanliness after the regional gathering.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 1:35pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. hands over the ceremonial wooden gavel to Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, marking the transfer of the ASEAN chairmanship on November 17, 2026.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos must also do their part to keep the streets clean after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in an interview with DZRH on Wednesday, November 18.

"Madalas naman nagki-clearing din ang Metropolitan Manila Development Authority, 'di ba? Kaya lang syempre 'pag nag-clearing ka, may magtatakbuhang mga illegal vendors. 'Pag may nangyari, ikaw na naman ang sisisihin. Ang paglilinis ng Pilipinas ay hindi lang sa gobyerno," Castro said.

(The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority often conducts clearing operations, doesn't it? But when you conduct clearing operations, some illegal vendors run away. If something happens, you get blamed again. Keeping the Philippines clean is not solely the government's responsibility.)
Her remarks came after cleanup and clearing operations for the 49th ASEAN Summit drew criticism, including allegations that the government was attempting to conceal poverty from visiting delegates.
Large fences and barriers featuring artworks by Filipino National Artists were installed along key motorcade routes in Pasay City.
Rep. Antonio Tinio (ACT Teachers party-list) alleged that the barriers were intended to hide poor communities from visiting delegates.
Some street vendors along these routes were also ordered to temporarily close their stalls for the duration of the summit.

The preparations have also drawn scrutiny over the P22.9 billion allocated for the Philippines' ASEAN hosting activities in 2026. Malacañang previously said the amount covers the country's yearlong chairmanship and related events, not just the November summit.
Castro reiterated the importance of personal responsibility in keeping the country clean, particularly through proper trash disposal.
"Sabi nila, 'Kaya niyo na mag-abroad pero 'yong magtapon ng basura sa tamang basurahan, hindi niyo magawa ... Dito lang napakadaming reklamo.'"
(They say, "You can afford to travel abroad, but you can't even throw your trash in the proper bin ... There are just so many complaints here.")
The 49th ASEAN Summit officially concluded on Tuesday, November 17, with the Philippines formally handing over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore for 2027.
Related engagements, including US President Donald Trump's visit, continued on November 18.

articles.title: COP31: Coastal areas must have a voice in ocean use, say PH officials
articles.summary: Coastal communities are supposed to be at the heart of the public process that allocates space for human activities in the waters

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Philippine energy and environment officials present at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Turkey hammered on the need for marine spatial planning to balance protection of marine biodiversity, coastal communities, with the need for renewable offshore wind and maritime economy.

Marine spatial planning is defined by UNESCO as a “public process” of “allocating the spatial and temporal distribution” of human activities, considering the impact on communities, the environment, and the economy.

A primary development concerning the ocean is offshore wind. The Philippines has a vast potential capacity for this, with 178 gigawatts (GW) of technical offshore wind potential. The national energy plan targets 19 to 50 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2050 under clean energy scenarios.

Energy Undersecretary Felix William Fuentebella said at a forum held in the Philippine hub at COP31 that they were working to strengthen “our offshore wind marine spatial planning goal and mitigation framework.”
Fuentebella emphasized the need to include coastal communities at the heart of this enterprise.
“Their participation should be made early, their knowledge must be part of decisions, and their communities should share clearly in the benefits of sustainable development,” said Fuentebella.

This was echoed by Shanelle Napoles of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources’ biodiversity management bureau during the forum: “[E]ffective marine spatial planning is guided not only by scientific evidence, but also by sound policies, clear institutional responsibilities, and meaningful participation of coastal communities.”
The process takes into account other sectors: maritime transport and shipping, tourism, fisheries, and conservation.
Not only will offshore wind help enable the Philippines to achieve its climate targets and speed up its green transition, this will also bolster the country’s energy security.

There is a push now at COP31 to integrate the ocean into the climate summit’s negotiations and final text. Alongside these efforts is the COP31 presidency’s electrification agenda in response to the global oil and fuel crisis.
A recent analysis from the World Resources Institute shows that coastal and island countries are leading the way.

Their analysis found that 95% of the nationally determined contributions of coastal and island countries include ocean solutions. WRI categorized the Philippines as including coastal and marine conservation in its climate targets. – Rappler.com

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth, and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

articles.title: Hontiveros, Alan Cayetano attend National Prayer Breakfast
articles.summary: Senator Risa Hontiveros and Senator Alan Peter Cayetano on Wednesday attended the 51st National Prayer Breakfast as guests of honor.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 1:24pm
Senator Risa Hontiveros and Senator Alan Peter Cayetano on Wednesday attended the 51st National Prayer Breakfast as guests of honor.
This year's theme is centered on "United in prayer, Healing our land."
During the event, Cayetano spoke about the problems currently facing the country, from political to economic, but acknowledged the power of prayer during this difficult time.

"Praying together with people you don't agree with, especially if it's people you don't like, is a good step forward kasi nawala yung national consensus. Parang nangyari ngayon palakasan na lang ng boses. We have to listen to each other. I really truly believe God will listen to us, but is also telling us to listen to each other," Cayetano said.
Hontiveros, meanwhile, urged the public to continue praying for them amid these challenges.

"There is something deeply comforting about knowing that in the midst of everything happening in our country there are people who take the time to pray for us... Kailangan po talaga namin, kaya pag patuloy po ninyo," Hontiveros said.
(We really need it, please continue praying.)
Hontiveros and Cayetano each received a Bible and were blessed with prayers from the community.
'Pray for our nation'
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also sent his message of support through a video message.
"As we seek God's wisdom may we find strength to serve with humility, act with integrity and lead with compassion," Gatchalian said.

Senator Bong Go also sent a video message saying that "prayer reminds us of the importance of humility, compassion and service to others, regardless of our different backgrounds and beliefs, to share a common hope for a peaceful, united and better Philippines."
Also in attendance were former chief justice Reynato Puno, Retired Associate Justice Raoul Victorino and Associate Justice Jhosep Lopez.

"Pray for our nation, pray as one, pray in harmony, pray as Filipinos for God's supernatural intervention, for wisdom, for integrity, for righteousness to guide the leaders of government, for our business leaders to have a heart for the poor. For our religious leaders to lift us to the high moral ground and for our people not to abandon hope for we have a God who is omniscient, omnipresent and omnipotent," Puno said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: House prosecutors reject Sara Duterte's 'honest mistake' claim on GenCorp SALN entry
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel has rejected Vice President Sara Duterte's claim that her declaration of GenCorp. Industries, Inc. as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 1:19pm

The House prosecution panel has rejected Vice President Sara Duterte's claim that her declaration of GenCorp. Industries, Inc. as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) could have been an honest mistake, saying she had repeatedly listed the company and its predecessors.

House prosecutor Joel Chua of Manila and prosecution panel adviser Robert Ace Barbers made the remarks in response to Vice Presidential spokesperson Paolo Panelo, who suggested that the inclusion of GenCorp. in Duterte's SALN could have been an honest mistake.

The Vice President is accused of betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution over allegations that she accumulated P817 million to P1.5 billion in unexplained wealth through the non-declaration of assets and failure to divest from businesses despite a constitutional prohibition.

“Somebody said the GenCorp. declaration was an honest mistake. But we have to remember, the Vice President declared GenCorp. as her business interest not for one year. She declared it for two consecutive years,” Chua said in an online press conference.
“Prior to GenCorp., she also declared other firms that eventually became GenCorp. as one of her business interests: Davao Bounty, Times Square, among others,” he added.

Chua also questioned the defense's claim that Duterte had no involvement in the companies, citing GenCorp.'s P33-million deal with the Davao City government, which is led by her brother, Mayor Sebastian Duterte.

“That's conflict of interest right there. And their witness said she received P2.1 million return of capital from GenCorp. Given these testimonies from their witnesses appear to testify against the Vice President,” Chua said.
Barbers, meanwhile, said the repeated declaration of the company in Duterte's SALN could not be dismissed as an honest mistake.

“Honest mistake for two consecutive years? If that was made by her staff member, that staff should be fired. Also, inadvertence will not exonerate or exculpate the Vice President from any liability,” Barbers said.
He also argued that Duterte was familiar with the history of the corporations that eventually became GenCorp., indicating that she knew about her investments in the company.

“Kabisadong kabisado ng Vice President ‘yung history… iyong mga prior corporation before the creation of GenCorp. Ibig sabihin, alam na alam niya ‘yung investment niya sa company niyan," Barbers said.
(The Vice President knows the corporation's history. That means she knows her investment in the company.)
"Hindi honest mistake yan. Iyong nagsasabi na ito yung honest mistake, para sa amin tingin namin ito yung palusot,” he added.
"That is not an honest mistake. For us, calling it an honest mistake is just an excuse.)
Defense witnesses have testified that Duterte had no business interests in GenCorp. and its predecessor companies, noting that her name does not appear in their corporate records.
The impeachment trial is set to resume on Thursday, November 19, with the defense continuing to present its evidence.— MCG, GMA News
