articles.title: Recollections of an Ifugao ambush
articles.summary: This is the story of how then-young governor Gualberto 'Bert' Lumauig braved the trauma and continued to serve — and be loved by his constituents — in Ifugao

blocks.text: BAGUIO, Philippines – I was five years old when my father, Governor Gualberto “Bert” Lumauig, was ambushed. We were living and studying in Quezon City. I remember visiting him in Veterans Hospital, where his room was cordoned off from media and guests, allowing only immediate family members inside his room. The ambush was on the headlines for days. Hundreds of telegrams of well-wishes were sent to him. Flowers and gifts were not allowed at all, apparently for security purposes.

I admired my Mom for her strength, ensuring Dad was cared for. Asking her years later how she took in all the violence that transpired, losing Uncle Jake and Uncle Peping, and leaving my Dad badly scarred. She said she held on to her faith and the utmost support of family and friends. Mom went with Dad during his six-month rehabilitation in the United States, but also made sure that we, their seven rambunctious children (ranging from ages 14 to 5), were left with able members of the family (a long list of aunts and uncles plus our grandparents).

July 23 every year thereon became a solemn day for the family, a day of quiet remembrance for the deaths of two people very close to Dad’s hearts: Uncle Jake and Uncle Peping, and surviving a violent attempt on our Dad’s life.

July 23, 1970. Bert Lumauig, who had just turned 37 years old, was the young governor of Ifugao. He presided over a meeting at the Banaue Hotel, a project he spearheaded which was scheduled to be inaugurated in two days. After dinner he, together with executive secretary Jake Dugyon, proceeded back to the capital town of Lagawe, about an hour’s drive from Banaue.There was a vehicle escort traveling ahead of them. Feeling exhausted, he slumped on his side at the back seat. Jake was on his left looking drowsy himself. Sergeant Manolo Domingo, his lone security, was seated directly in front of him beside his cousin Jose “Peping” Bacani, who was behind the wheel.

It was pitch dark and a bit foggy when they climbed up the driveway from the hotel to link up with the national road. They barely traveled two kilometers away from the hotel and negotiating a road bend when a volley of gunfire pierced the night’s silence and bullets rained on their car.

Instinctively he slid down from his seat to the floor. He tried to pull down Jake with his left arm but immediately stopped when bullets all but severed his arm. Jake moaned “Lord,” then pitched forward against the front seat’s backrest.

Gunfire continued without let-up. Bullets peppered his heavily padded winter jacket. He desperately fought to stay conscious and, as he did so, he thought he saw the likeness of the Virgin Mother and, from the depths of his heart, he whispered over and over the “Memorare,” the prayer his mother taught him in his youth.

He drifted back and forth from consciousness and unconsciousness, remembrances flashing like water in an onrushing stream that dropped in an eddy and whirled at no fixed direction, tears swelling his eyes as he asked what wrong had he committed against his people to deserve this barbaric attempt on his life. On their lives.

Gunfire seemed unstoppable. Bullets grazed his two ribs, a grenade shrapnel was embedded in his upper right head, and his upper right arm and back were bleeding. He managed to slowly crawl out of the left car door, weak but emboldened until he collapsed in a water-filled deep canal along the road.

Raul Casumpang, interpreter of the local Court of First Instance in Lagawe, was rushing to Banaue that night in his private jeep to visit a seriously ill relative. He met the speeding escort and was told about the ambush. Himmediately mobilized residents of the nearby sitios to come to their rescue. Upon reaching the ambush site, governor Lumauig was not in his car, so Casumpang walked a few distances until he came upon the governor’s helpless body profusely bleeding on the canal.

Casumpang rushed the governor to the nearby Good News Clinic and Hospital, a non-stock, non-profit religious mission hospital in Tam-an, Banaue. In and out of consciousness, governor Lumauig remembered pleading to the doctor and nurses, “Please do not cut off my arm,” as he seemed to feel his left arm dangling from the extensive bullet wounds, hanging by the cartilage and flesh.

“Try not to speak, Sir,” said the doctor, who he learned later was Dr. Romulo Emlano. Assisting him were two young ladies, one from Mayoyao, Norma Bongyo (who would later become his goddaughter in marriage when she got married to provincial engineer Sarol of Banaue), and Florence Cayong, from Banaue.
“The others, Jake, Manolo, Peping,” he weakly repeated.
“Sir, you’re badly wounded,” was the reply he got from Dr. Emlano.

He could hear calls for blood donors since he was losing so much blood. Rushing to his bedside was then-barangay captain Juan Tillay. He offered to donate all his blood just so the governor would be saved. He also refused to leave the clinic, fearing that the gunmen would somehow return, knowing the governor had survived.

His eyes became heavy, thinking of his wife Felicisima and the kids. He hoped none of his people would exact “revenge” and touch off a bloodbath in his beloved province. Then he drifted into a deep sleep.

Seeing the severity of the injuries and without much equipment in the clinic, Dr. Emlano immediately suggested for the governor to be airlifted to Manila. It was late at night and the possibility of flying was impossible, so at the break of dawn governor Lumauig was flown from the Good News Clinic to Veterans Hospital in Quezon City, where he underwent surgeries amid security concerns. His left arm was saved, but it was badly scarred, and he lost any sensory abilities on the lower arm and fingers.

It was only days later that he learned that his executive secretary, Jake Dugyon, a model family man and devout Christian, and his cousin-driver, Peping Bacani, did not survive the ambush. Sergeant Domingo sustained bullet wounds in his legs and was immediately treated.

The extent of the governor’s injuries required him to undergo further medical procedures in the United States, where he spent six months of surgeries, physical rehabilitation, and psychological therapy. It was only upon his return to the Philippines when Banaue Hotel — a project he envisioned, tirelessly secured resources for and steadfastly pushed for its successful completion — was finally inaugurated.

Upon his return to Banaue, he made sure that he visited the Good News Clinic and Hospital to personally express his extreme gratitude to Dr. Emlano, the nurses, and staff for saving his life. Throughout the years thereafter, he championed GNCH’s work, from procuring medicines through Manila-based pharmaceutical firms to encouraging philanthropic partners to invest in the clinic’s mission.

Led by then-Criminal Investigation chief Colonel Ernesto Cariño, the ambush was thoroughly investigated. It was discovered that there were seven foxholes in the ambush site, plus 75 empty shells of varied high-powered automatic rifles and two grenade safety pins.

There were also empty sardine tin cans and bread wrappers, indicating the ambushers were prepared for a long wait to accomplish their killing mission. There were arrests made, where one gunman confessed and named the alleged mastermind behind the dastardly deed.

Then-President Ferdinand Marcos offered the governor to join the diplomatic service with an ambassadorial position, perhaps with the assumption that the ambush had discouraged governor Lumauig from seeking another political term. He respectfully requested the President to allow him to consult his local leaders. The President agreed, and even invited him to bring the leaders to Malacañang.

The governor brought his trusted advisors Eladio Malingan, Santiago Habawel, Santiago Balajo, Jose Guinid, Amado Bokiagon, and some of the mayors. In the audience with the President, they were vehement in their objection to governor Lumauig leaving the leadership of Ifugao.

Despite veteran political personalities out to ease him out, Lumauig trounced his rival for governor with an avalanche of votes by the grateful people of Ifugao, appreciative of his performance and service. He went on to became assemblyman and congressman of Ifugao, selflessly serving his beloved province for another two decades.

I had thought that the ambush was already behind him decades later, especially after noticing that he was no longer hiding his ugly scars on his left arm, wearing short sleeve polos in public. But when he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s dementia in 2016, one of his nightmares in the middle of the night was dark memories of that fateful night in 1970. While I was by his bedside, he would start shouting repeatedly, “Protect your Mom, there are men after us!” I had to assure him that Mom was quietly sleeping beside him.

The progression of his dementia caused traumatic memories of the ambush to re-emerge, making events from decades ago seem vividly present once again. These moments that made me scared, upset, and melancholic. I knew things would get worse than better, but at the same time I had to remain optimistic for his sake.

Eight years ago on November 18, 2018, we lost our Dad. He had been in and out of the hospital for years, and his physical body just gave up. From that ambush in 1970 where his left arm was shattered, to his Parkinson’s disease where his right hand had uncontrollable tremors, and progressing to dementia where traumatic memories creeped on him relentlessly, we had to accept that his time on earth was up, and that God needed another angel in heaven. – Rappler.com

The author based most of the narrative of the ambush on the book Into the New Horizon: Ifugao, written by her father, the late Gualberto “Bert” Lumauig, published in 2008. A reprint will be available soon.

Good News Clinic and Hospital, which remains the only hospital in Banaue, Ifugao, is fighting to continue its mission too. It is raising funds through a sale of donated artworks until December 6, 2026.

SEOUL, South Korea – US and South Korean authorities have issued cybersecurity advisories, urging Java users to urgently install security updates after vulnerabilities were found in the popular programming language.

Such was the concern in South Korea, where Java is widely used, that the presidential office held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, November 17, with related government agencies to discuss preemptive measures to tackle the issue, the Yonhap news agency reported.

Java, available from Oracle as well as from open-source Java development kits, is used in critical information systems spanning government agencies, the corporate sector and financial institutions as well as the military.
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said in an advisory that the vulnerabilities required immediate patching.
Oracle could not be immediately reached for comment, but it issued a software update for its Java Development Kit on November 17 that contains fixes for the issue.

Cybersecurity concerns around the world have mounted this year with the rapid pace of AI development, including rogue AI agent incidents, and amid a slew of tech outages in recent days. Cybersecurity companies regularly turn up examples of hackers using AI to launch scores of intrusions at once.
South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and the Korea Internet & Security Agency said on Wednesday that public institutions and private enterprises must urgently install the security updates.

South Korea is considered to be particularly vulnerable as it is among countries with heavy Java usage rates across the public and private sectors, according to a 2021 survey by the programming tool maker JetBrains.
China and Germany also have heavy usage rates.
Java represented 53% of programming language use in South Korea compared to a global average of 30%, the JetBrains survey said.
The use in South Korea was especially high in the public sector with a 72% share of programming language use for information systems, according to a government survey last year. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Who is Timor-Leste's dancing prime minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão?
articles.summary: Xanana Gusmão's dancing drew cheers at ASEAN, but his political career stretches back to Timor-Leste's decades-long struggle for independence.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 1:08pm

MANILA, Philippines — He danced with Filipino performers to the beat of P-pop group SB19, drew cheers from fellow Southeast Asian leaders and became one of the crowd favorites at the closing ceremony of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila.
The man was Timor-Leste Prime Minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão, who joined performers dancing to SB19's rendition of "Together in Motion," the official theme song of the 2026 ASEAN Summit.
But it was not the first time he danced during his visit. He also joined in when Filipino young artists welcomed him upon his arrival and showed off a few moves during the summit's opening night.

But Gusmão is known for more than his dancing. Before becoming prime minister, he led the armed resistance against Indonesia's occupation of East Timor, spent years in prison and later became the country's first president after independence.
From journalist to resistance leader
Born on June 20, 1946, in Manatuto, Gusmão grew up when Timor-Leste was still under Portuguese rule, according to the Timor-Leste government's official biography.
He worked in public administration before joining the Portuguese military. He later became a journalist and photographer for the newspaper A Voz de Timor.

His involvement in the independence movement began in 1974, when he joined the Timorese Social Democratic Association, which later became the Revolutionary Front for an Independent East Timor, or FRETILIN.

Indonesia invaded East Timor on Dec. 7, 1975, shortly after the territory declared independence from Portugal. The occupation led to years of armed resistance and a long struggle for self-determination.
Gusmão became one of the leading figures in that resistance. After the death of FRETILIN leader Nicolau Lobato in 1978, he helped reorganize the movement.
In 1981, he was elected leader of the resistance and commander-in-chief of its armed wing, the Armed Forces for the National Liberation of East Timor, or FALINTIL.
He also worked to unite different groups seeking independence. In 1988, he helped establish the National Council of Maubere Resistance, which later became the National Council of Timorese Resistance.
Imprisonment and independence
According to the Timor-Leste government's official biography, Indonesian forces captured Gusmão on Nov. 20, 1992, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

His arrest did not end his involvement in the independence movement. He continued to communicate with resistance leaders while in detention and used his time in prison to study Indonesian, English and law. He also wrote poetry and painted.
He was transferred to house arrest in February 1999 and released on September 7 that year.

Months earlier, on Aug. 30, 1999, East Timorese voted in a United Nations-backed referendum on whether to accept an autonomy proposal within Indonesia. A majority rejected the proposal, paving the way for the end of Indonesian rule.
Timor-Leste became an independent country on May 20, 2002, and Gusmão was elected its first president.
He served until 2007, when he became prime minister. He returned to the post in 2012 but resigned in 2015, saying he wanted to give younger leaders an opportunity to take over.

Gusmão remained involved in government, later serving as minister of planning and strategic investment. He also led negotiations with Australia over maritime boundaries, which resulted in a treaty ratified in 2019.
He returned as prime minister on July 1, 2023, after his party, the National Congress for Timorese Reconstruction, won the parliamentary elections.
Timor-Leste's decades-long bid to join ASEAN
Timor-Leste's push to join ASEAN began decades before it became the bloc's 11th member.

President José Ramos-Horta has been among the country's strongest advocates for regional integration. He discussed the idea with then-Indonesian Foreign Minister Adam Malik as early as 1974, when Timor-Leste was still under Portuguese rule.

Ramos-Horta, who served as president from 2007 to 2012 and returned to the post in 2022, also helped advance the country's bid for membership. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996 for his work toward a peaceful resolution of the conflict in East Timor.
Timor-Leste formally applied for ASEAN membership on March 4, 2011, during Ramos-Horta's presidency, with Gusmão then serving as prime minister.
The application, however, did not lead to immediate membership. ASEAN had to assess whether the young country had the resources, personnel and institutions needed to meet the bloc's commitments.

In November 2022, ASEAN leaders agreed in principle to admit Timor-Leste and granted it observer status. They later approved a roadmap in May 2023 to help the country meet the requirements for full membership.
Under Gusmão's government, Timor-Leste worked to comply with the requirements across ASEAN's political-security, economic and socio-cultural pillars.
Philippines backs membership bid
The Philippines has supported Timor-Leste's bid to join ASEAN since 2002, with successive administrations maintaining the country's position.
Former president Benigno Aquino III also pledged support for Timor-Leste's membership in 2013.
In May 2023, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assured then-Timor-Leste Prime Minister Taur Matan Ruak of Manila's support during a meeting on the sidelines of the 42nd ASEAN Summit in Indonesia.
"In the Philippines, you have a partner. We have always been supportive," Marcos said.

Marcos reiterated this during Timorese President José Ramos-Horta's state visit to the Philippines in November 2023. Ramos-Horta said the two countries shared a "long history of solidarity and support for each other."
The Philippines maintained its support even after a diplomatic disagreement with Timor-Leste over the extradition of former Negros Oriental congressman Arnolfo Teves Jr.

In March 2025, a Timorese court rejected the Philippines' request to extradite Teves, who faces multiple murder charges, including over the killing of former governor Roel Degamo. The Philippine government criticized the ruling, saying it went against the trust and cooperation expected among ASEAN members.
In May 2025, the Philippines again expressed support for Timor-Leste's membership ahead of the 46th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur.

Then Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Theresa Lazaro said Manila had committed to supporting Timor-Leste's accession and helping implement the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 following a preparatory meeting on May 24.
The Philippines' renewed assurance came just two months after the disagreement over Teves.
Timor-Leste becomes ASEAN's 11th member

ASEAN leaders agreed to admit Timor-Leste during the bloc's 47th summit in May 2025. The country formally became the 11th member on Oct. 26, 2025, during the 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
Gusmão signed the declaration on Timor-Leste's admission, while Ramos-Horta attended the ceremony.
Timor-Leste was the first country to join ASEAN since Cambodia in 1999. Its entry also meant the ASEAN emblem, which features rice stalks representing its member states, would have an 11th stalk.
The Manila summit in November 2026 was Timor-Leste's first full ASEAN summit as a member of the regional bloc. — with reports from Cristina Chi, Ian Laqui, Helen Flores and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Marcos: No Pax Silica signing during Trump's ASEAN visit
articles.summary: The Philippines will not sign the Pax Silica agreement during US President Donald Trump's visit for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on…

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 1:02pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines will not sign the Pax Silica agreement during US President Donald Trump's visit for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Wednesday, November 18.
The agreement would formalize the country's participation in the US-led initiative to secure global semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains.

Lee Lipton, US ambassador to the Philippines, earlier said that there would be no announcement on the project during the ASEAN Summit this month, but the country's Board of Investments expects the signing to take place before the end of 2026.

Under the agreement, a 4,000-acre industrial center would be built in the Luzon Economic Corridor, beginning with a 1,620-hectare site in New Clark City, Tarlac, which has drawn criticism over alleged environmental degradation and the displacement of farming and fishing communities. The Philippines hub would be the first site developed among members of the Pax Silica consortium.

The Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities has described messaging surrounding the initiative as "mixed," saying that important details, such as control over the hub and its products and its environmental impact, remain unclear even as negotiations progress.
Pax Silica is also being oversimplified into an “arms race” between the US and China, organization Executive Director Angelo Kairos dela Cruz said.

Several progressive groups, including renowned Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, have called for the rejection of the project. Protests against Pax Silica have also been held during the summit.

Over 200 individuals were arrested at a protest against the initiative and Trump's visit in Sucat, Muntinlupa, on Sunday, November 15. The 276 protesters, including at least 50 students from the University of the Philippines system, were in police custody for more than two days at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City after a delay in inquest proceedings.
In a report of GMA News, the National Capital Region Police Office said the detainees' transfer to the detention facility was being processed.

articles.title: ‘Human’ wins Cambridge dictionary’s word of the year
articles.summary:
Meaning and use of word has become more important in age of AI chatbot, says dictionary

In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary…

blocks.text: In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human.

Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.

AI advances have spurred questions about whether computers can achieve consciousness, with the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins among those who answered in the affirmative, saying he was “left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human”. Sceptics, on the other hand, argue that there is a vast difference between how a human brain evolves and how an AI system is built.

Cambridge dictionary said the meaning and use of “human” had become more important in the age of the chatbot. Colin McIntosh, an editor of the dictionary, said AI was “changing the way we talk about being human” and had led to the word of the year being deployed to distinguish our work from that of advanced computer systems.

“Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking has made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children,” he said. “A recent increase in compounds such as ‘human-made’ highlight how the word has come to distinguish works or qualities of people, as distinct from AI.”

Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.”

Other tech-related words were on the shortlist: “agent”, the term for an AI system that can operate – sometimes alarmingly – without human control, and “analogues”, relating to non-digital activities. A non-tech contender was “wholesome”, a word to describe something which is likely to improve your life either physically, morally, or emotionally.
Earlier this month, “mogging” – meaning to outperform or outshine someone or something – was named the Collins word of the year.

Tech-adjacent words also stood out among the new additions to the Cambridge dictionary. “Looksmaxxing”, describing the act of making oneself as physically attractive as possible, which has been associated with the online manosphere, and “aura farming”, another term often encountered on social media, which refers to “the activity of doing things with the intention of showing a personality that people admire and think is attractive and interesting”.
after newsletter promotion

The former UK prime minister Keir Starmer made the news late last year when some social media users wondered “why he was aura farming” with his TikToks; Andy Burnham also appears to be attempting to master the art after becoming prime minister.

articles.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
articles.summary:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to…

blocks.text: The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

blocks.caption: A street scene in Cairo.  Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
after newsletter promotion
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

blocks.caption: A customer pays for tomatoes with Egyptian pound banknotes at a market in Cairo. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Drinking beer and spirits raises risk of acute kidney damage, study suggests
articles.summary:
Research also shows consuming wine could cut risk, reopening debate on whether beverage has health benefits

Drinking beer and spirits increases the risk of serious kidney damage, whereas…

blocks.text: Drinking beer and spirits increases the risk of serious kidney damage, whereas consuming wine offers protection against it, a study suggests.
People who drink nine units of spirits a week are 26% more likely to suffer acute kidney injury than those who consume only one unit a week.
Beer lovers are also at higher risk. Those who drink 24 units of beer a week are 15% more likely to develop the condition than those who consume three units weekly.
In contrast, drinking fewer than 14 units a week of either red or white wine does not raise the risk of kidney damage. In fact it appears to reduce it.
The findings, published in the journal Scientific Reports, have reopened the longstanding debate about whether drinking wine offers health benefits.

The academics behind the research, from Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge, acknowledge in their paper that “the relationship between alcohol consumption and acute kidney injury (AKI) is controversial”.
They analysed data detailing the health of 250,791 adults from the UK Biobank study who drank alcohol and followed them over a period of 14 years.

Although beer and spirits increase the risk of acute kidney injury, Dr Rudolph Schutte and colleagues also found that wine drinkers become exposed to the same risk if they consume more than 14 units a week, the maximum alcohol intake recommended by the UK’s chief medical officers.

They concluded that there is “a direct relationship between alcohol consumption and AKI”. However, they stressed that they had only found an association between them and could not prove that the relationship is causal.
“Acute kidney injury is a serious condition that can lead to chronic kidney disease, kidney failure and an increased risk of dying early,” said Schutte.

“While alcohol has traditionally been linked with kidney injury through its impact on the liver, our research suggests that spirits and beer may contribute directly to kidney damage through inflammatory pathways.”
They found that those with a higher risk of AKI had higher than usual levels of an inflammatory marker called C-reactive protein and a raised neutrophil count.
“Spirts and beer appear to drive these inflammatory markers while red wine and white wine showed inverse protective relationships,” they said.
after newsletter promotion
“Even consuming less or equal to 14 units per week captured from spirits [was] associated with an increased risk for AKI.
“Conversely, no associations existed between red wine, white wine and AKI, except for a protective tendency of red wine consumption in men and when consuming less or equal to 14 units per week.”
Dr Peter Rice, the chair of the Institute of Alcohol Studies, urged caution about the interpretation of studies that find that red wine is healthier than other forms of alcohol.
“Studies which examine the health impacts of different alcoholic beverages are difficult to undertake due to a number of factors,” he said.
“In general, wine consumers tend to have fewer dietary and activity risk factors and are more affluent.

“The effect of the alcohol molecule on body tissues does not vary with the type of alcoholic product, therefore any difference in health outcomes is often due to other risk factors, in particular deprivation.”

articles.title: Trump 'not concerned' about South China Sea as he meets Marcos in Malacañang
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump said he was not concerned about the situation in the hotly contested South China Sea.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 12:54pm
US President Donald Trump speaks at the ASEAN-US Special Summit on Nov. 17, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — United States President Donald Trump said he was not concerned about the situation in the hotly contested South China Sea.

“I’m not concerned at all. That’ll be taken care of,” Trump said at the start of bilateral talks with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday, November 18, hours before flying to China to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump also told reporters that the US alliance with the Philippines "has never been better" and that Washington and Manila were expanding their defense cooperation.

articles.title: Trump not concerned by WPS tensions, says issue will be 'taken care of'
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he was not concerned about tensions in the West Philippine Sea, adding that the issue would be “taken care of.”

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 12:41pm
United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he was not concerned about tensions in the West Philippine Sea, assuring that the issue would be “taken care of.”

"I'm not concerned at all. I'm not concerned about that at all. That'll be taken care of," Trump said when asked by a reporter how concerned he was about the maritime tensions and how prepared the United States was under its Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) with the Philippines.

Trump made the remark during his bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang, where the two leaders reaffirmed their countries' longstanding alliance and discussed areas for greater cooperation.
The US president was in Manila on November 17 and 18 for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits.

During their opening remarks, Marcos described the United States as the Philippines' only treaty ally, noting that the two countries are marking 80 years of diplomatic relations and 75 years of their alliance under the MDT.

Trump, meanwhile, said the two countries were expanding their defense cooperation, citing increased US foreign military financing for the Philippines and the approval of more than US$5 billion (approximately P250 billion) in arms sales since he took office.
"America stands with the Filipino people just as we have for generations. We've been your ally, but not as close as it is now," Trump said.
The MDT, signed in 1951, commits the Philippines and the United States to come to each other's defense in the event of an armed attack on either country.
During the treaty's 75th anniversary, Washington reaffirmed its commitment to supporting the Philippines in monitoring its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and upholding its defense interests.
Tensions in the South China Sea have persisted amid China's expansive maritime claims, which overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia.

On July 12, 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that China's sweeping claims over nearly the entire South China Sea had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). Beijing has rejected the ruling.— MCG, GMA News

The protesters marching along Recto Avenue stopped at a police barricade at San Sebastian Street, where they held a program. Around 11 a.m., the protesters were seen running along Recto Avenue.

articles.title: Wages grow at fastest pace since 2023 – but prices are climbing even more quickly
articles.summary:
Wage rates climb about 1 percentage point faster than before pandemic, triggering warnings of a sixth RBA rate rise

Wages grew at their fastest pace since late 2023 over the three months to…

blocks.text: Wages grew at their fastest pace since late 2023 over the three months to September, buoyed up by this year’s boost to minimum pay rates for millions of lower paid workers – but still not fast enough to keep up with the rising cost of living.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ wage price index climbed by 1.1% in the most recent quarter, lifting the annual increase to 3.5% – a pace that economists said would keep the Reserve Bank on edge about the need for further interest rate hikes.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the pickup in wages growth was thanks to the government’s support for the minimum pay rise.
“We’re helping to deliver higher wages for workers because we know this is one of the best ways to help with the cost of living,” he said.
While wage rates are climbing about 1 percentage point faster per year on average than before the pandemic, prices are climbing even more quickly – a reality that Chalmers recognised.

“Real wages are declining not because wages have been too low but because inflation is still too high, which is why helping in the fight against inflation and getting the budget in better nick are such high priorities for the government.”
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the latest figures confirmed that “Australians are working harder for less”.
“Australians are poorer under Labor. That is the reality of the economy that has been built by a Labor government that simply does not get it,” he said at a press conference.

items: Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

blocks.text: The Fair Work Commission in early June implemented a 6% pay rise to about 100,000 of the country’s lowest paid employees to help compensate for cost of living pressures made worse by surging fuel prices.
The annual review also gave a 4.75% pay rise to 2.7 million workers on award wages.
Rachael McCririck, head of prices statistics at the ABS, said these decisions “were a key driver of much of the growth in private sector wages this quarter”.
Analysts said wages were growing faster than the Reserve Bank had been expecting, and that this added to the case, if only at the margin, for a potential sixth interest rate hike.

Cherelle Murphy, EY’s chief economist, said she did not expect a move after the RBA’s final board meeting for the year on 7-8 December, even though the wage growth figure was “uncomfortably high for the central bank”.
“[It’s] unlikely to prompt any immediate reaction, given the economy is now slowing in response to the five interest rate hikes delivered between February and November this year,” Murphy said.
“We expect the central bank will be in wait-and-see mode,” she said.
The ABS figures showed pay rates are rising fastest in the public sector, up by an annual 3.9%, while private sector wages increased by 3.4%.

“The main driver of public sector wage growth was pay rises for state government frontline workers covered by enterprise agreements. This included groups like nurses, midwives and police officers,” McCririck said.
Wages after inflation

Jeff Borland, an economics professor at the University of Melbourne, said while the wage price index was useful to assess inflationary pressures in the labour market, it was less useful as a way to assess workers’ actual incomes.

“The WPI is the labour cost to an employer of having a particular job done. If you want to know what is happening to the average worker, then the weekly income from the [ABS’s] characteristics of employment survey is a better measure,” Borland said.
By this broader measure of worker pay, the story is not as dire as that told by the after-inflation change in the WPI, he said.
Real average hourly labour income received per employed person was artificially boosted through the pandemic but has since come back to be just 3.4% higher this decade.
This extends the overall weak trend through the 2010s, Borland said.
In contrast, the wage price index is down 4.4% since the start of 2020.
“None of the real wage measures are telling you things are going gangbusters,” Borland said.
“But there’s a difference in the degree to which they tell you how badly things are going.”

articles.title: ‘Aarigaa!’: the triumph of Mary Peltola’s historic US Senate win and what it means for Alaska Natives
articles.summary:
Peltola, the first Alaska Native in the US Senate, ran a campaign that drew universal issues from her own Indigenous politics

Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states…

blocks.text: Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton Hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters.

It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senate candidate from expressing her elation, bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.
Before she could speak, a volunteer shouted out from the back of the hall: “Aarigaa!” Peltola picked up the refrain, and threw it right back:
“Aarigaa! Can we just chant aarigaa? Aarigaa! Aarigaa!”
It was just one word. But it encapsulated something special about Peltola and her insurgent’s campaign to unseat the incumbent Republican US senator, Dan Sullivan.

“Aarigaa” is an Iñupiaq word that is commonly understood across Alaska’s 229 federally recognised tribes. It is a word of celebration, of relief almost, that roughly translates to: “Way to go!” or “Attaboy!”
Now, Peltola genuinely has a reason for exclaiming it. On Tuesday – two weeks after the midterm elections – the tortuous count was finally completed, and she was declared winner.
In prevailing, she becomes the first Alaska Native to take a seat in the US Senate.

blocks.caption: Mary Peltola during a campaign rally at the Alaska Aviation Museum in Anchorage, Alaska, on 30 October. Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I was so happy at that moment,” said Ana Hoffman, a lifelong friend of the senator-elect’s who was present in the Sheraton ballroom. “Aarigaa! It demonstrated through language what her campaign is all about: inclusion, representation, identity.”

The last US Senate race of the 2026 cycle to be called, Peltola’s victory carries with it several layers of significance. For US politics as a whole, it awards Democrats comfortable control of the upper chamber of Congress, with 56 seats to Republicans’ 44.

For Native Americans across the union, it marks the first time that seven Native people will be serving simultaneously in Congress – representatives Josh Brecheen and Tom Cole from Oklahoma, Sharice Davids from Kansas, Sean McCann from Michigan and Claire Valdez from New York; and senators Peggy Flanagan from Minnesota and Peltola from Alaska.
And for Alaska Natives, there is their own resounding cause to roar aarigaa: since Congress was convened 237 years ago, there have been more than 20,000 seats filled in the US House and Senate.

Among them, only 29 have been occupied by Native Americans, and of those Peltola is the only Alaska Native to have served in Congress. She won Alaska’s only House of Representatives seat in 2022, losing it two years later to the Republican Nick Begich, and in January she will take her Senate seat as part of the new intake.

Hoffman, who is president of the Native Corporation in Peltola’s home town of Bethel in western Alaska, said that her friend’s victory would uplift a people “who have been marginalized and underrepresented throughout generations. ‘Alaska Native’ will no longer be a concept in the Senate, it will be a colleague.”

blocks.caption: Supporters cheer as Mary Peltola speaks during an election-night watch party at the Sheraton Hotel in Anchorage on 3 November. Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

blocks.text: The gaping lack of representation of Alaska Natives is no small thing for Alaska or the US. Alaska is home to about 40% of all federally recognized tribes in the union, and the one in five voters who are Indigenous amount to the largest proportion of the electorate in any state.

“Alaska Natives have played pivotal roles in US history, around decisions on land, resources and development. Yet their centrality to US decision-making still takes many people by surprise,” said Sonja Castañeda Dower, a congressional fellow with the American Political Science Association who has studied the power of Alaskan tribes.

Peltola is a Yup’ik Alaskan from Bethel, a town of fewer than 7,000 people that acts as the hub of 56 villages scattered along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers. Her Yup’ik name is Akalleq, or “the one who rolled”. Her mother was from the nearby community of Kwethluk; her father, a German American, came to Alaska from Nebraska to work as a pilot.

As a young girl, Peltola began fishing the Kuskokwim river with her father from the age of six. “We’d pass each other on the river,” said Hoffman, who lives in Bethel and is also Yup’ik. “We had fish camps near one another along the same slough.”

Peltola put Alaska Native issues and sensibilities at the center of her election campaign. She made exceptional efforts to reach out to communities that have rarely been included in the political process, travelling by floatplanes, four-wheelers and snowmachines to far-flung parts of the last frontier – a state that is larger in landmass than California and Texas combined.
Peltola showed up in more than 50 communities, some with a population of fewer than 300 people.

blocks.caption: Campaigners outside Midtown Mall in Anchorage on 2 November. Photograph: Christian Moorman/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Yup’ik symbolism was embedded in her campaign. At campaign stops, she wore mukluk boots and Indigenous kuspuk shirts. The campaign’s circular logo was modelled on the Yup’ik eye, a traditional sign that also alludes to the eyewear made from wood or walrus ivory worn by Yup’ik people as protection against the blinding glare of the arctic snow.

“Peltola leaned into her Yup’ik identity as a qualification for advancing policies that appealed to a broad base of Alaskan supporters,” said Elise Blasingame, a political scientist specialising in Native American representation at Emory University, and a citizen of the Osage Nation. She added: “Look at her campaign’s merchandise. Who else would market a baby onesie saying: ‘I teethe on dried salmon’?”

You might also ask, who else would put salmon at the heart of an electoral contest for national office? The official mantra of the campaign was “Fish, family, freedom” – a slogan that neatly captures the dual nature of Peltola’s message and can be read in equal measure as an appeal to Native tribal people and as a paean to Alaskan and American patriotism.

Fish embody that double-edged message. As Peltola explained in an interview in October, about 80% of the diet of Yup’ik people has traditionally been fish, of which about half is salmon. “Our generic word for fish is the generic word for food,” she said. “Neqa.”

The devastating decline of the catch of chinook salmon, or king salmon, along the Kuskokwim river in recent years, partly as a result of the climate crisis and partly through over-trawling in international waters in the Bering Sea, is an existential challenge for Alaska Native tribes. Their villages are sited on riverbanks along the salmon run.
“Fish, and our access to them, are the reason our communities exist,” Hoffman said.

But fish are also central to the entire economy of Alaska, Indigenous or not. The state accounts for about 60% of all wild seafood harvested across the US, and the combination of subsistence fishing, industrial fish processing and tourism is critical to Alaska’s 740,000 residents as a whole.

So when Peltola made a central pitch of her campaign that her rival, the incumbent Republican senator, was selling out the people in favor of big trawler companies, it spoke not just to the 20% of the electorate who are Alaska Native, but to all Alaskans. Without that, she would never have stood a chance – she had to reach the independent and wavering Republican voters who overwhelmingly elected Donald Trump in 2024 and for whom Native issues are not top priority.

Peltola, like Democrats across the country, hammered the issue of affordability on the campaign trail. When a gallon of milk costs as much as $21 in the most isolated parts of the state, and grocery prices are sky-high as a result of Donald Trump’s war with Iran, that is a concern for all Alaskans.
For Hoffman, that is the key to Peltola’s agonisingly delayed victory – she drew out of her own Indigenous politics what was universal for every voter.
“That’s the beauty about Mary, that she understood the universality of who we are as Alaskans. So the focus on access to fish, for Alaskans, that is like the pursuit of happiness.”

In the end, though the race was tight, Sullivan could not overcome that universal appeal. The furor over the appearance of a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot, which the New York Times revealed just weeks before the election had been a ruse cooked up by Democratic operatives aligned with the Peltola campaign, provided the Republican incumbent with ammunition late in the cycle.

blocks.caption: Mary Peltola at the Alaska Aviation Museum on 30 October in Anchorage, Alaska. Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Sullivan backers also rolled out their own dirty tricks. In September, the Republican-linked Senate Leadership Fund Pac put out an ad titled: “Who is Mary Peltola?” It featured a middle-aged white man saying: “They dress her up, throw her out on a stream somewhere, make her look like an Alaskan.”

In case the racial undertone of that comment was too subtle for some viewers, the ad went on to hear from a white woman: “Every time Mary Peltola gets in a room with her people, she’s not with our people,” the woman said.

That pandering to Alaska Native otherness ultimately failed. Though detailed figures are not yet available, anecdotal evidence suggests that a surge in Alaska Native turnout contributed to Sullivan’s loss.
In her election night speech Peltola name-checked one of her fellow Yup’ik residents in Bethel, Susan Murphy. The Guardian reached out to Murphy, 85, by phone.

She said that on election day she passed the polling place near her house several times. It was in a parking lot, and each time she walked by she saw the lot full of voters standing patiently in line.

It was reminiscent of a scene in Bethel on 26 August 1958. She was 17 on that day, and still in high school. The town was much smaller then. “There were only about 500 Bethel residents then,” she said.
A similarly impressive proportion of the town turned out to the polls that August. They were voting for statehood, for Alaska to become the 49th state of the union.
Now there is a chance of forming a more perfect union with the arrival of Peltola in the US Senate. “It is important, of course it is,” Murphy said. “It is a start.”

articles.title: Amid learning crisis, PH to lead ASEAN bid to boost reading, math skills
articles.summary: While developing ASEAN's learning recovery plan, the Philippines will also have to ensure that its own ARAL Program has enough funds to effectively help struggling Filipino students

blocks.text: ARAL PROGRAM. Pupils attend a remediation session under the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning Program at the Senator Benigno S. Aquino Jr. Elementary School in Manila, May 26, 2026.
Second Congressional Commission on Education
While developing ASEAN's learning recovery plan, the Philippines will also have to ensure that its own ARAL Program has enough funds to effectively help struggling Filipino students

items: ASEAN aims to enhance reading, math, and socio-emotional skills across member states, as outlined in the ASEAN Declaration on Foundational Learning.
The Philippines will lead initiatives such as the ASEAN Academic Recovery and Catch-up Program to address learning gaps and improve education standards.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) will move to improve reading, math, and socio-emotional skills of students in the region, according to the Philippine Department of Education (DepEd).
It is the core of the ASEAN Declaration on Foundational Learning (ADFL), adopted during the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila.

By making foundational learning a regional priority, the 11 member states of ASEAN will support early learning, inclusive education, learning recovery, teacher development, responsible use of technology and artificial intelligence, data-driven policies, and sustained investment.

“This declaration goes beyond high-level policy; it is our shared commitment across Southeast Asia to make sure every young learner gets the early support they need to succeed,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said on Monday, November 16.
“When we strengthen fundamental learning in our classrooms today, we are directly opening doors to real jobs, practical skills, and a brighter future for our youth.”
Under the Philippines’ 2026 ASEAN chairmanship, the DepEd proposed the ADFL in February. It has since undergone extensive regional consultations.

The pitch came amid the Philippines’ attempts to reverse its decades-long learning crisis, documented through national literacy surveys and dismal performances in global evaluations such as the Programme for International Student Assessment.
The ADFL is just one of the boxes to be ticked under the ASEAN Work Plan on Education 2026-2030. The Philippines will take the lead in ensuring that the regional bloc is implementing the plan.
Aside from this, the Philippines will design and disseminate the ASEAN Academic Recovery and Catch-up Program (ARC-UP), with a timeline of 2027 to 2029, according to the work plan.
The DepEd said ARC-UP will serve as an “integrated regional mechanism” to enable ASEAN member states to share data, target resource allocation, and scale proven strategies to address learning gaps.

While developing ASEAN’s learning recovery plan, the Philippines will also have to ensure that its own Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning or ARAL Program has enough funds to effectively help struggling Filipino students.
The Philippines is also tasked with leading the development of standards for the professionalization of early childhood care and development workers.

“Although access to and completion of primary and secondary education have expanded significantly, foundational learning remains highly uneven across the region, with large disparities across countries and education levels,” according to the ASEAN work plan.

The document states that Singapore, Vietnam, and Malaysia reported over half of their students meeting minimum proficiency benchmarks in reading and mathematics at the primary level, with “Singapore’s rates near universal and Vietnam performing particularly well” in math.
It added that several other ASEAN member states, including Laos, Myanmar, and Cambodia, have less than 20% of students reaching the minimum proficiency level.

According to the PISA 2025 results, 15-year-old Filipinos had performance gains in reading, science, and mathematics. The DepEd partly attributed these gains to the implementation of the ARAL Program. Still, work continues as the Philippines remains ranked in the bottom 20.
Not all ASEAN member states participated in the latest round of PISA, which is administered by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
Cambodia’s PISA trajectory is similar to the Philippines’, posting improved scores but still having more than half of tested students classified as low-performing.

The co-lead for the ADFL is Cambodia, which will contribute to the formation of regional models by sharing Phnom Penh’s experiences on teaching methods as well as literacy and numeracy strategies, among others.
According to the work plan, Cambodia will also pilot a catch-up program model and document learnings for regional replication.

Observers will now look to how Singapore would be moving forward education reform talks during its ASEAN chairmanship in 2027. Singapore’s PISA 2025 results showed a decline in reading scores, reflecting the global trend. – Rappler.com

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. and US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said Wednesday that there will be no signing of the Pax Silica initiative during US President Donald Trump's state visit in the Philippines.
"There'll be no signing," Lipton said.
"No, not on this trip. We are not doing it. We are not covering that on this trip," Marcos said.

Officials have clarified that there will be no data centers included in the Pax Silica initiative, as its main objective is to process the country’s minerals and make high-tech components for AI and semiconductors.

articles.summary: A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison for his role in plotting to kill US politicians, including President Donald Trump.

image.caption: The man was arrested in 2024 when Trump was running for reelection [FILE: October 13, 2026]Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A US court sentenced a Pakistani man to more than 27 years in jail for plotting to kill US President Donald Trump and other prominent politicians at the behest of Iran, authorities said on Tuesday.

"Not many charges … are more serious than the contemplated, targeted killing of a US president or other senior government official," said US District Judge Eric Komitee while reading out the sentence.

The 48-year-old man was handed 330 months in prison for "attempting to commit an act of ​terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire," the US Department of Justice said in a ​statement. That's 27 years and six months.
A US jury had already convicted the man in March of traveling to the US to arrange political assassinations on American soil.

The trial had begun in late February, days before the Trump administration ordered strikes on Iran that it carried out with Israel. The war has killed thousands, mostly in Iran, Lebanon and Yemen, but also in countries around the Persian Gulf.
It is still ongoing.
A plot to kill Trump: What prompted it?

Prosecutors said the convict tried to recruit people in the US for a plan to kill Trump and other US politicians in retaliation for Washington's killing of Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani in January 2020.
Trump was in his first term as US president at the time.
Other targets in the 2024 plot included then-US President Joe Biden and Nikki Haley, who ran against Trump for the Republican presidential nominination, prosecutors said.
What else do we know about foiled plot to kill US politicians?
During his trial, the man testified that he had joined the plot with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps but did so unwillingly to protect his family in Tehran.
Tehran has denied targeting Trump or other US officials or plotting attacks against them.

The Pakistani man bluntly told jurors that he researched Trump's rally locations and spoke of carrying out an assassination at a political rally to an acquaintance. He then lined up people he thought were hit men and paid them $5,000 in cash that he had borrowed from a relative.
The man also said that he assumed that US authorities would foil the plan, that he would cooperate and that he might get immigration help as a reward.
The DOJ said that a person contacted the man in April 2024 to help with the plot, only to report his activities and become a confidential informant.
The convicted man was arrested in Texas in July 2024, a day before an unrelated attempt on Trump's life in Butler, Pennsylvania.

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

articles.title: Mary Peltola wins U.S. Senate seat in Alaska for Democrats
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent's name and…

image.caption: Mary Peltola, the Democrats' candidate for the U.S. Senate in Alaska, is seen arriving for a mid-term election night party in Anchorage, Alaska, on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent's name and completing a political comeback in a state U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.
Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin in Senate after Alaska win

The Alaska race is the last U.S. Senate contest to be resolved in this year's midterm elections, and Peltola's victory expands the Democrats' majority after they retook control of the chamber. The party already won campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and, most recently, Mississippi.
With Peltola's victory, Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most since 1958. Republicans entered the midterms with a 53-47 majority, while Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin.
Messages seeking comment were left with both campaigns Tuesday night.

items: Mississippi's Scott Colom secures Senate seat in another midterm win for Democrats
Ohio and Texas went from red to blue in the midterms but may not stay that way in 2028

blocks.text: Peltola, in a statement on social media, said there "is no greater honour than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs and put Alaska first. Thank you, Alaska. Let's get to work."
Peltola previously held the state's lone House seat. She lost her bid for a second full term to a Republican in 2024, but she became central to Democrats' plans to retake the Senate in 2026.
Two candidates named Sullivan
In the campaign's final stretch, however, she faced allegations that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent.
Trump called for Peltola's prosecution after the New York Times first reported the allegation less than a week before the Nov. 3 election. Peltola denied any involvement.
"I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent," Peltola told supporters in Juneau days before the election.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola's campaign or running at the Democrats' behest. He has not responded to messages from The Associated Press since the Times article was published.

The Times report was based partly on text messages and other documents and interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, who was fired shortly before this year's open primary and later sought to recant her statements. But the second Sullivan had already been on Trump's mind. He referred to him multiple times during a rally in support of the senator in mid-October.

Later, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit that Trump said he ordered. It sought to block certification of the race if the incumbent were to lose, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Peltola called the lawsuit "flagrant corruption."

The case was dismissed by a federal judge, but the Justice Department appealed. Attorneys for the state sought dismissal, saying officials should be able to conduct the election "without unwarranted interference by the United States." They also argued the ballot was designed to distinguish the two Sullivans as much as possible and that Alaska's ranked choice voting process would allow any voters who might be confused to rank them.

articles.title: Apec summit live: Xi and Putin speak as world leaders gather in China
articles.summary: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin

blocks.text: Key events

items: 14m agoApec opens in China's tech hub Shenzen

blocks.text: Rebecca Bailey
We’re back for day two of the Apec CEO Summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen. Today the summit will be addressed by APEC leaders, with President Xi Jinping set to give a keynote speech.

Bilateral meetings will continue on the sidelines, although the most eye-catching – Xi and Donald Trump, and the US-China-Russia trilateral – won’t be until Thursday. Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen this morning, greeted by a red carpet, soldiers and pom pom-waving dancers dressed in fuchsia and blue. Communist party politburo member Cai Qi, often described as Xi’s right-hand man, was there to meet him.

blocks.caption: Vladimir Putin arrives in Shenzhen ahead of Apec. Photograph: Anupam Nath/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Trump will leave Manila, where he has been attending the Asean forum, later on Wednesday. The Associated Press reports that he has expressed excitement about his own welcome ceremony: “I hear we’re going to have quite a landing,” he told reporters. “It’s going to be a beautiful thing.”
Aside from the high-level hobnobbing, delegates are “working around the clock” to agree on a joint statement for Thursday, a senior Apec official told Reuters on Tuesday.
Carlos Kuriyama, director of the Apec policy support unit, said all 21 Apec members agreed on the need to ensure trade is “not only open, but also fair”.
He said they were also discussing the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence.
double quotation markThey are working very hard to make sure that we can have a common language.”
Apec opens in China's tech hub Shenzen

It’s been a big week already for diplomatic summits, with the most anticipated among them, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leader’s meeting, starting today in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzen.
Some observers have noted that we could be about to witness a Yalta 2.0, a reference to a major 1945 wartime conference attended by Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.

That’s because the leaders of the US, China and Russia – namely Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin – will meet for trilateral talks at the summit to discuss the wars in Iran and Ukraine, denuclearisation, economics, tech and trade.

blocks.caption: Xi Jinping and leaders pose for a group photo at the start of the Apec summit.  Photograph: Pedro Pardo/EPA

blocks.text: Trump has also floated the possibility of meeting North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term.
Here is a quick recap of the latest before the event kicks off:

items: China’s foreign ministry said the leaders “will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”. The ministry added that: “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”

The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.” But it has dismissed comparisons with the 1945 Yalta meeting saying they were just “games of political scientists”.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

articles.title: Held beyond legal limits? Lawyers seek dismissal of ASEAN protest raps
articles.summary: The National Union of Peoples' Lawyers has filed motions seeking the dismissal of complaints against protesters.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 11:45am

Protesters clash with police officers during a demonstration that coincides with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Leaders' Summit and Related Summits in Manila on Nov. 15, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The National Union of Peoples' Lawyers (NUPL) has asked prosecutors to dismiss complaints against protesters arrested during the ASEAN summit, arguing that they were detained beyond the period allowed by law and denied their right to the speedy disposition of cases.

NUPL chair Edre Olalia told Philstar.com that the group filed the motions before the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office on behalf of protesters arrested in Sucat, Muntinlupa City, on Sunday, November 15.

Olalia said the motions were based on the protesters' continued detention beyond the maximum allowed period without the timely filing of complaints, as well as alleged violations of their right to the speedy disposition of cases.
He also confirmed that law enforcement officers had asked protesters whether they wanted to waive their rights under Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code, describing such inquiries as "routinary."
Article 125 sets the time limits for bringing people arrested without a warrant before the proper judicial authorities.
The law provides detention limits of 12 hours for offenses punishable by light penalties, 18 hours for correctional penalties and 36 hours for afflictive or capital penalties.
A detainee may waive these limits to undergo a preliminary investigation instead of an immediate inquest. Such a waiver must be voluntary and executed with the assistance of legal counsel.
Complaints against protesters
More than 200 protesters were arrested in separate demonstrations across Metro Manila on Nov. 15, as Southeast Asian leaders gathered in the Philippines for the 49th ASEAN Summit.

According to a STAR report, protesters arrested in Muntinlupa, mostly members of Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan, underwent inquest proceedings over alleged violations of Batas Pambansa 880, or the Public Assembly Act, as well as alarm and scandal, and resistance and disobedience to persons in authority.
Nine protesters faced additional complaints for grave coercion and malicious mischief over allegations that they broke into a convenience store and damaged property.

Meanwhile, eight activists arrested at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila underwent separate inquest proceedings for alleged tumult and other disturbances of public order, direct assault and illegal assembly.
The motions filed by NUPL concern the protesters arrested in Muntinlupa.
The filing of criminal complaints before prosecutors does not necessarily mean charges have been filed in court.

articles.title: ‘Everyone likes money’: Bandidos member can’t remember why he was paid $165,000, Big Build inquiry hears
articles.summary:
Commissioner says inference could be made that bikie Joel Leavitt was ‘standing over’ union-aligned labour hire firm for the payment

A Bandidos gang member says he couldn’t remember a…

blocks.text: A Bandidos gang member says he couldn’t remember a lucrative invoice because it brought up bad memories of having been told there was a contract out on his life.
Former CFMEU member and bikie, Joel Leavitt faced a second day of examination by the royal commission into alleged corruption across Victoria’s construction sector on Wednesday.
Questioning returned to a $165,000 invoice paid to Leavitt’s now defunct company, JVL Consulting, by union-aligned subcontractor BK Labour Hire in July 2025.
When shown a copy of the invoice Leavitt was unable to recall anything to do with it, or even give a clear answer as to what services his former company provided.
Counsel assisting the commission, Chris Carr SC asked why Leavitt appeared to become uncomfortable when asked about the invoice.
Leavitt blamed his poor memory on having ADHD, as well as PTSD from being shot in May 2023.
“Around that time I actually got told by gang squad that there was a contract on my life,” he said.
“So it brought back some uncomfortable memories.
“That’s why I blocked out a lot of that time.”
Commissioner Chris Kourakis AC warned Leavitt it was an offence to fail to answer questions put to him by the commission, something he said could ultimately be tested in a courtroom.
“I’ve been shot … I’ve had drug issues … I am answering these to the best of my recollection,” Leavitt replied.
“How do you think you would act if you’d ever been shot?”
After the commission briefly adjourned for Leavitt to speak with his lawyers, the bikie returned to the stand saying JVL Consulting provided safety advice to companies.
“Maybe helping them out with their procedures and policies and stuff like that,” he said.
The commission viewed a copy of Leavitt’s bank statement at the time which fluctuated between $0, down to minus $20, before the $165,000 landed in his account.
“Everyone likes money. I’m sure all youse are on good money for this,” said Leavitt, addressing the bar table.
Kourakis informed Leavitt the commission had evidence he did not do any work for BK Labour.
He said an inference that could be made is Leavitt was “standing over” BK Labour for the payment because he needed money.
“If that’s the way you want to look at it commissioner,” Leavitt replied.
Carr asked if Leavitt knew something about BK Labour that the company would have wanted to keep quiet.
“Is the conclusion the commission should draw is that you just stood over them with some sort of explicit or implied threat of violence?” Carr asked.
“I’d like to talk to my counsel before I answer that,” Leavitt replied.
The inquiry continues.
