articles.title: Australia’s ‘problematic’ surrogacy laws could be transformed under proposed changes
articles.summary:
Law reform body recommends ongoing ban on commercial surrogacy, but greater compensation for surrogates, and safeguards around who the child’s legal parents are

  • Get our

blocks.text: Surrogates would be entitled to full compensation, with a nationally consistent framework ensuring domestic surrogacy is a viable option to parenthood, under proposed changes by Australia’s law reform body.

The Australian Law Reform Commission has been investigating how to better regulate surrogacy and harmonise laws so they are consistent with international legal obligations, while protecting human rights – particularly the rights and best interests of the child.

On Tuesday evening, it tabled its 47 recommendations, with the aim of making the process easier to access while ensuring the safety of all parties. These include licensed surrogacy support organisations to help intended parents connect with surrogates, greater compensation for surrogates and greater safeguards around who the child’s legal parents are.

“Good surrogacy laws should do two things: enable people to form families through surrogacy where it can be undertaken responsibly; and provide effective safeguards against exploitation and harm. Our current laws do not achieve either aim,” the ALRC’s president, Justice Mordy Bromberg, said.
“Instead, they drive Australians to pursue overseas surrogacy arrangements, which can expose children, surrogates and intended parents to great risk of harm and exploitation.”

The review found that inconsistent surrogacy laws and criminal sanctions are driving parents overseas and arrangements underground, making them “less visible, increasing rather than reducing the risk of harm”.

While the exact number of surrogacy births is hard to determine, estimates suggest that domestic gestational births more than tripled over the recent decade, from 27 births in 2014 to 84 births in 2023, the report found.

Overseas surrogacy also increased substantially over a similar period, from 246 in 2015 to 375 births in 2024, an increase of more than 40% – suggesting surrogacy is becoming a more significant pathway to family formation because it has occurred while the overall birthrate has fallen, the report said.

The report recommended that while a ban on commercial surrogacy should stay in place, surrogates should receive greater compensation to cover medical costs, loss of earnings including superannuation, birth support and other costs incurred by the pregnancy.
The report found the “problematic nature of Australian surrogacy laws” is a major driver of intended parents going overseas, where the risk of harm and exploitation is at its highest.
after newsletter promotion
ALRC’s principal legal officer, Jacinth Pathmanathan, said the report calls for lawful, well-regulated overseas surrogacy.
“Under the recommended framework, intended parents would need to take several steps before entering an overseas arrangement,” Pathmanathan said.

“They would have to register, receive official guidance and obtain legal advice in both Australia and the overseas country. They would also need to take reasonable steps to avoid arrangements that are unlawful in the overseas country, don’t meet minimum Australian requirements or that pose significant risk. Failing to meet these obligations could result in a civil penalty.”
The Australian Law Reform Commission’s report and its recommendations are now with the commonwealth attorney general for consideration.

articles.title: What Filipinos can learn from ASEAN Prize 2026 recipient Hla Hla Aung
articles.summary: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has recognized a Myanmar geologist and seismologist as recipient of this year's ASEAN Prize.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 11:28am
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has recognized a Myanmar geologist and seismologist as recipient of this year's ASEAN Prize.
Hla Hla Aung was recognized for her continued commitment to advancing disaster resilience, particularly in turning scientific research into policies and community empowerment.
In an interview, Hla Hla Aung shared experiences that Filipinos can learn from regarding earthquake response.
Limited studies on earthquakes? That did not stop Hla Hla Aung from learning and sharing information to help communities.
She, instead, read English articles and then translated these into the Myanmar language.

"I used to read books from the foreign countries, articles written by the foreign experts. Then, I have to use the experience from these books and articles for the Myanmar earthquake," the ASEAN Prize recipient said in an interview.
At 80, Hla Hla Aung still continues her advocacy to promote disaster preparedness and resiliency. MARIEL CELINE SERQUIÑA/GMA News

Hla Hla Aung serves as patron of the Myanmar Earthquake Committee of the Myanmar Engineering Society, which aims to enhance earthquake preparedness, seismic hazard assessment, and structural safety throughout Myanmar.
She did not just stop at learning about earthquakes from foreign studies but also translated her learnings from English to the Myanmar language and published these in local newspapers.
"So if people know about earthquakes, they will build strong houses to avoid the damage during the disaster," Hla Hla Aung said.
For 20 years since 1969, Hla Hla Aung has dedicated herself to advancing disaster resilience, even giving demonstrations at schools and monasteries.
One thing she emphasized during the interview is the importance of duck, cover, and hold.

"I demonstrate. You just hold, cover your head, drop under the table, and then you just hold on the leg of the table or bed, and you stay there until you have help from outside. That's the way," Hla Hla Aung said.
"So, I demonstrate to the monastery students, and to other school," she added.
Now 80 years old, Hla Hla Aung continues her advocacy to push for a disaster resilient community.
"You cannot get this (ASEAN Prize) only one, two, three years [but] 20 years. I'm still doing the same thing," Hla Hla Aung said.
"I'm writing articles because I want people to know what to do when earthquake occurs. Then you can save the lives of the people," she added.
Established in 2018, the ASEAN Prize is an annual regional award that recognizes and celebrates outstanding achievements by ASEAN citizens. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Mary Peltola beats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska to give Democrats 56 Senate seats
articles.summary:
Republican incumbent beaten in race dominated by controversy over second candidate named Dan Sullivan

Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican…

blocks.text: Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.

Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.

Alaska was the last Senate race remaining to be called, and with Peltola’s victory, Democrats will control 56 seats in the upper chamber. The party as a whole gained nine Senate seats in the midterms, a sweeping victory that will put them decisively back in the majority beginning next year, when they are expected to embark on an aggressive campaign of both lawmaking and investigating.

Peltola faced significant controversy on the campaign trail, after the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in a scheme to recruit another Republican challenger, also named Dan Sullivan, to appear on the ballot.

Peltola’s campaign had denied any involvement in encouraging the second Sullivan’s run, and after state election officials tried to remove him, Alaska’s supreme court in June ruled he be allowed to appear on the ballot. Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted over the apparent ruse, and Alaska’s top federal prosecutor announced that criminal and civil inquiries were under way, while the state’s governor separately announced plans to open a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme.
Though Alaska is a Republican stronghold in presidential years, Peltola was viewed as a uniquely potent challenger to Sullivan, a two-term senator first elected in 2014 after defeating a Democrat.

A former state legislator who grew up in small communities along the Kuskokwim River in Alaska’s interior, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022, when she won a special election to replace the longtime Republican at-large congressman Don Young following his sudden death, and became the first Alaska native elected to Congress.

Peltola won a full term later that year, but lost re-election to Republican Nick Begich in 2024. She then entered the race against Sullivan, and her fortunes appeared to rise as Alaskans grew frustrated with the price increases brought on by Trump’s tariffs and his decision to attack Iran earlier this year.

The state is the largest in the union, and dotted with cities and villages that are disconnected from the road system, and thus particularly hard-hit by the increases in oil prices the war caused. Gas prices in some interior Alaska communities jumped into the double-digits per gallon, while the rise in the price of diesel affected everything from groceries to alcohol, since many communities rely on shipments by sea.

Alaska is nonetheless a right-leaning state heavily reliant on its fishing and oil and gas industries. On the campaign trail, Peltola adopted the slogan “fish, family, freedom” to highlight how she would stand up for the state’s unique interests in Washington DC.

She has cast herself as an advocate for expanding oil production in the state, and addressing the issue of bycatch, or the accidental fishing of unwanted species, which some Alaskans believe is to blame for declining salmon runs.

Peltola, who is Yup’ik, will join Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe, as the first two Native American women to serve in the US Senate. Late in her campaign, Peltola posted a photograph of herself on Instagram from 1995, wearing the winner’s sash from the Miss National Congress of American Indians pageant. “Then and now, Alaska is at the heart of who I am,” she wrote.

Sullivan, meanwhile, stuck to Trump’s side, even as the president’s popularity declined nationwide, and especially in Alaska, according to some surveys. He did not join other vulnerable Republicans in urging an end to the war with Iran, while accusing Peltola of disrespecting voters after a report emerged that she had used a hompohobic slur and abused her staff.

articles.title: NUPL: 276 arrested ASEAN Summit protesters, journalists file motion for release
articles.summary: A lawyers' group on Wednesday said they filed a motion before the Muntinlupa City prosecutor seeking the immediate release of 276 protesters and journalists arrested during a protest amid the opening…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 11:17am

A lawyers' group on Wednesday said they filed a motion before the Muntinlupa City prosecutor seeking the immediate release of 276 protesters and journalists arrested during a protest amid the opening of the ASEAN Summit 2026.
In a motion filed Tuesday, the National Union of Peoples' Lawyers (NUPL) has also asked for the dismissal of the complaints against the arrested individuals.
NUPL chairperson Edre Olalia confirmed the document to GMA News Online on Wednesday.
The lawyers argued that the continued detention of the respondents for more than 36 hours without the filing of charges before a court constituted a continuing violation of their fundamental rights.

They said the Philippine National Police (PNP), which filed the complaints against the arrested, failed to submit the required evidence within the period prescribed under Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code.
The provision requires authorities to bring persons arrested without a warrant before the proper judicial authorities within 12, 18, or 36 hours, depending on the gravity of the offense.
As of the filing of the motion, the respondents had allegedly not received copies of the complaint-affidavits, witness affidavits, or other evidence.
Despite their continued detention, no information had been filed against them before any court, the lawyers said.
“No less than the 1987 Constitution provides that no person shall be deprived of liberty without due process of law,” the motion read.
NUPL also cited the respondents' right to a speedy disposition of cases, arguing that the inquest proceedings should not be used to justify prolonged detention beyond the periods allowed by law.

Also, NUPL questioned the legality of the arrests, saying many of the respondents were merely exercising their constitutional rights to free speech, peaceful assembly and to seek redress of grievances.
Earlier, the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) said that the arrested protesters are set to be transferred to a detention facility.
NCRPO chief Police Brigadier General Christopher Abrahano said authorities are waiting for commitment orders from the court.

“Finile na po natin ang kaso. Nakalagak na po sa prosecutor's office ‘yung kasong finile natin at pinoproseso na lang po ang pag-transfer sa detention facility,” he told GMA News’ Unang Balita in an interview.
(We have filed the case. The case has been filed with the prosecutor's office and the transfer to the detention facility is currently being processed.)
“Ngayon pa ay nandoon sa Camp Bagong Diwa 'yung ating mga naaresto at any time probably, makapag-issue na ng commitment order 'yung korte,” he said.
(The arrested protesters are still at Camp Bagong Diwa and any time probably, the court will issue a commitment order.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Pinoy recruited for alleged foreign military job intercepted
articles.summary: In a statement on November 18, the Bureau of Immigration said that it intercepted a man at Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 on November 7 as he attempted to board a flight to Vietnam for…

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 11:14am
Bureau of Immigration Building in Intramuros, Manila
Elmer B. Domingo via Wikipedia
MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Immigration has intercepted another Filipino who was allegedly bound for a military job outside the country.

In a statement on November 18, the Bureau of Immigration said it intercepted a man at Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 on November 7 as he attempted to board a flight to Vietnam for a purported job with a foreign military.
According to the bureau, the passenger was flagged for secondary inspection after immigration officers noticed inconsistencies in his travel documents and statements.
During further questioning, the man revealed that he had responded to a Facebook advertisement promising a monthly salary of over P100,000, along with a $10,000 signing bonus.
A foreign recruiter subsequently moved their communications to WhatsApp and covered his airfare and other travel expenses.
The passenger eventually admitted that tourism was not his true purpose for traveling.

After assessing him as a potential victim of human trafficking or illegal recruitment, BI officers turned the passenger over to the Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking for further assessment and assistance.
The Bureau of Immigration has also intercepted Filipinos in previous months who were allegedly recruited for military, border guard or armed conflict zone jobs.
All cases involved the same scheme, which offered a signing bonus in foreign currency and a six-digit monthly salary in pesos.

articles.title: Slovakia: Thousands protest against pro-Kremlin leader Robert Fico
articles.summary: Prime Minister Robert Fico has been under fire over his ties to Russia. The rallies were held on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that toppled communism in Czechoslovakia.

image.caption: Some 25,000 people turned out in Bratislava to join protests against the pro-Russian government of Robert FicoImage: Tomas Benedikovic/AFP

blocks.text: Thousands of people protested across Slovakia on Tuesday to demonstrate against Prime Minister Robert Fico and his pro-Russian government.
The demonstration was organized by opposition parties and non-governmental organizations (NGOs).
The largest protest was on SNP Square, which was the site of the main anti-Communist protests during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, in the capital, Bratislava.
Organizers said 25,000 people had gathered there.
Other rallies were also held across the country, which is an EU and NATO member​​​​​​, including in the cities of Kosice and Banska Bystrica.

blocks.caption: Robert Fico was the only serving EU leader to visit Moscow for the annual Victory Day parade this yearImage: Ramil Sitdikov/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why are people protesting in Slovakia?
The rallies were held on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended decades of communist rule in what was then called Czechoslovakia.
Protesters commemorated the fall of the communist dictatorship, which ruled Czechoslovakia for 41 years. They also called for more support for Ukraine.
The demonstrators mostly focused on Slovakia's prime minister, however, chanting slogans such as "We've had enough of Fico!"
One banner told the prime minister to "Go to hell."
Slovakia amid deepening political and social strains
Why are Slovaks angry with Fico?
Since Hungary's Viktor Orban was removed from power in April, Fico stands as Europe's most pro-Russian leader.
He opposed military aid for Ukraine and has maintained close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite European Union sanctions against Russia.
Fico, who has served as prime minister four times in over two decades, has faced numerous protests since returning to power in 2023.
Fico has also repeatedly clashed with the EU. Last year, Slovakia's constitution was amended to state that national law takes precedence over EU law.
He has also been criticized for trying to exert greater control over the media and culture, and curbing LGBTQ+ rights.
"We're the last ones in the European Union to be negotiating with the Russians... It's a disgrace," Igor Vico, a 74-year-old doctor, told AFP.
"We're at the bottom of the world, not just in Europe, and it makes me sad," he said.

articles.title: The ‘moon landing’ of gaming: Australians, some of the first to play GTA VI, prepare to descend on Vice City
articles.summary:
After a 13 year wait for the latest Grand Theft Auto instalment, Thursday’s launch is shaping up to be ‘the biggest gaming event that’s ever been’

Gamers across Australia are preparing for…

blocks.text: Gamers across Australia are preparing for the once-in-a-generation release of Grand Theft Auto VI, a day acolytes of the franchise say will be bigger than the biggest sporting events.

Details surrounding GTA VI, set in the fictional world of Leonida and its metropolis, the Miami-esque Vice City, have been scarce. But Rockstar Games has been building hype for months, driving supercars along Florida streets, planning a music festival and drip-feeding clips to a ravenous public.
With a global release time of the stroke of midnight on Thursday 19 November, Australians will be able to access the game second only to New Zealanders.
Joe Randle, an online creator known as ToastedShoes, said the game’s release was an unprecedented moment for the industry.
“It is by far the biggest gaming event that’s ever been,” he told Guardian Australia. “It’s not like the Super Bowl, that happens every year. I would probably call it the moon landing of gaming.”

Like other streamers, Randle will go live on Twitch just before the game drops and stream for hours into the night, with videos set to drop on YouTube shortly afterwards. Business aside, the release is an “incredibly exciting” time to be a fan.
“It’s a little bit surreal almost, like it’s too good to be true” he said. “I’ve waited years for this.”

The scale of the release is staggering. Rockstar hasn’t released any public figures, but it’s thought the game cost upwards of $1.5bn to develop. Estimates for preorders are approaching 16m copies, meaning the game has already brought in more than $2.2bn in revenue before its launch.

Analysts say that number could jump to $4.5bn to $7.5bn in its first week and keep climbing, figures that are even more stunning considering the game’s age restrictions: It’s rated 17+ in the US and R18+ in Australia, meaning it’s legally restricted to adults aged 18 and over.
NBN Co, the federal enterprise that operates the country’s broadband system, said data suggested Thursday will be a massive moment for Australian gamers.

Last Thursday, the first day people could pre-download the GTA VI, saw a new record set for the level of traffic on the NBN network. Every second, the equivalent of 57 days of full HD streaming video flowed through the NBN, about 10% higher than average.
In total, NBN said the excess data amounted to about 330,000 downloads of GTA VI since the preload period began.

Matt Judge, an Australian streamer with nearly a million Twitch followers under the handle DarkViperAU, has built a career within the world of Grand Theft Auto 5. The game came out in 2013, and in the intervening years Judge has spent more than 13,000 hours in the fictional world of Los Santos, based on Los Angeles.
GTA VI has promised to build on the good will Rockstar has cultivated with the franchise and beloved games such as the Red Dead Redemption series, he said.

“Waiting that long for anything obviously is going to build a lot of anticipation and hype,” Judge said, saying he has been adjusting his sleep schedule to get ready for a playing marathon, shifting his wake-up time from around 8.30am to 3.30pm. “There was some expectation that the game would be released in 2018, it’s not only that we’ve waited 13 years but we’ve waited eight years longer than we expected.”
As a fan, Judge can’t wait to immerse himself in the world of GTA VI. But as a creator, he’s a little daunted.

“A lot of what made me be successful online was my immense knowledge of the single player version of GTA V,” he said. “But now I’m starting on the ground floor with everyone else in a new world that I don’t know as well … that makes me a bit nervous.
“Everyone recognises that a new hit game could be your meal ticket.”

Maggie Brennan, a tattoo artist from Victoria who streams under the handle retromaggie, said the impending release feels like the drop of the year’s biggest action movie, paired with a major musical release. A 34-song soundtrack comes out on Friday.

“As a big fan of the GTA series, tomorrow’s game release is really exciting for myself and other gamers who have loved the worlds that Rockstar games have created,” she wrote in an email, adding the community surrounding the game had helped her deal with her own personal health struggles.
“I have made a lot of friends along the way.”
Will you be playing? What are your plans for the release? Email Nick at nickvisser@theguardian.com

articles.title: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI
articles.summary:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams

The integrity of South Korea’s…

blocks.text: The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.

On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.

The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.

But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.

Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.

In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”

blocks.caption: South Korean education minister Choi Kyo-jin reviews the method used to cheat in the national tax accountant exam. Photograph: Seo Dae-yeon/YONHAP/AP

blocks.text: His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.

The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.

Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.

Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.

The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.

blocks.caption: Workers process packages of question-and-answer sheets for South Korea’s university entrance exams on 16 November. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA

blocks.text: Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.

To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title: Would AI have come up with a better word of the year than the Cambridge Dictionary?
articles.summary: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence.

image.caption: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen 'human' as its 2026 word of the year. (Nathan Howard/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence.
The publication has chosen 'human' in response to concerns around artificial intelligence
The choice announced Wednesday in the U.K. highlights the debate over how AI blurs the lines between machines and people.

Explaining the choice, the dictionary said, "Throughout history, the adjective human has signified people, as opposed to animals and gods (and, more recently, machines). Increasingly seen in compounds such as human-written, human-generated, and human-made, it now also denotes that something is created by or typical of people as opposed to AI."

Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer, notes that though AI has been a growing presence in society for years, in 2026, it seemed to be everywhere — and changed how people talk about being human.

"2026 has been all about a refound appreciation of the human factor in what we consume (with a consequent human premium)," he said in a statement, "and a new value is being placed on the human element in our lives in general: all confirmed by our analysis of the language data, internet trends, and search habits."
Given that, he said, human was the perfect choice.
He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back

Last year's word of the year was also AI-related. Cambridge Dictionary chose "parasocial," explaining that "as social media intensifies the intimacy that fans feel with their adored celebrities, and with the rise in popularity of AI companions that can take on personalities, the word for these one-way relationships — parasocial — is having its own moment."
Four other words made the shortlist for the 2026 word of the year: analogue, agent, wholesome and chic.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Tag team: dual waterspouts appear in San Francisco Bay amid stormy weather
articles.summary:
Phenomenon is not a common occurrence in the Bay area and inclement weather is expected to continue for few days

A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area,…

blocks.text: A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area, much to the delight and shock of several observers, as storms pummelled the region.

Two waterspouts – vortexes of air and water mist, essentially tornadoes – cut a sheer streak into the sky, as they spiraled above the bay, according to social media footage capturing the weather phenomenon.
While prevalent in the Great Lakes and the south-east Floridian coast, waterspout sightings are not common for the Bay area, according to federal storm data.

The National Weather Service (NWS) confirmed the waterspout occurrence in a Monday special marine warning. Some waterspouts, dubbed “fair weather”, are weak, while others, typically tornadic waterspouts can pose a risk to boaters and coastal areas if they travel on shore.

The inclement weather is set to continue for a few more days. According to an NWS forecast, the Bay area is predicted to be drenched in rain on Tuesday with potential thunderstorms on Wednesday and Thursday.
Elevated tide levels raise the risk of coastal flooding through at least Thursday, according to the agency.
Powerful wind is also forecasted with East Bay Hills expected to see gusts reaching up to 70mph (112 km/h).
After Thursday evening, the showers may subside with some rain lingering over the Pacific and its adjacent inland communities.

articles.title: One Nation says it would cut Australia’s refugee intake by 90% under ‘tough stance’
articles.summary:
Pauline Hanson opens new war of words on immigration as foreign minister Penny Wong accuses populist party of ‘dividing Australians’

  • Get our

blocks.text: One Nation has vowed to cut Australia’s refugee intake by 90% and scrap the permanent parent visa program under its latest hardline plan to slash migration.
Pauline Hanson announced the policy on Tuesday labelling it a “tough” approach to migration.
The rightwing party said if it held power it would cut the refugee program from 20,000 places per year to 2,000 and claimed Australia would still remain above the OECD average for places per capita.
One Nation’s push would end Australia’s status as one of the most generous refugee programs behind Canada.
“The cost [to] … the taxpayer is enormous. The cost is, on average, about $500,000 a year in a lifetime of expenditure per person in the country,” Hanson told reporters.

“We’ve got to take a tough stance on this. My concern is for these people out there … that are doing it tough. You don’t bring more people into the country if they cannot fund their own bed or hospital beds.”

Hanson claimed her plan would save the budget more than $140bn over 10 years. Migrants from countries on the Albanese government’s “do not travel” list, including Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Somalia, would still be banned from entering the country.

One Nation says analysis based on Treasury modelling, adjusted for inflation, found the lifetime cost of a humanitarian entrant was $523,000. Treasury modelling done in December 2021 found the cost was $400,000 with 90% of it borne by the federal government.
Labor has committed to retaining the refugee intake at 20,000 per year while the Coalition has promised to halve it to 10,000.

The foreign minister, Penny Wong, accused One Nation of trying to divide the country. She said Australia had the right balance and questioned Hanson’s claim that Australia would remain above the OECD average under the minor party’s plan.

“I don’t accept those figures and I find when Ms Hanson speaks, you always have to check what is actually being said. There are countries which take more refugees, there are countries which take fewer. We think this [20,000 per year] is the right balance,” Wong said.

“We have unprecedented people movement around the world. We have displacement of more human beings than at any time since world war II. We make a very small contribution to that by our refugee intake.”
after newsletter promotion
Wong said it was “more of the same” from One Nation.
“I know that they think dividing Australians is the best response to the politics of the time,” the Labor frontbencher said. “I take a different view.”
Other nations including the US and Canada have tightened their migration programs in recent years with Canada reducing its parent visa program.
Hanson said One Nation was not barring migrant parents from moving to Australia, but they would have to be sponsored, or could visit their families on temporary visas.
“We’re not saying parents can’t come out … [but] they will actually be sponsored by the families not the taxpayers.”

articles.title: What Trump said and did in his first hours in Manila
articles.summary: The US president used his stop in manila to set the agenda for China and the Quad while reassuring Southeast Asian leaders.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 8:36am

MANILA, Philippines — US President Donald Trump used a brief stop in Manila to rally Indo-Pacific partners around security, critical minerals and trade after arriving past 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, November 17.
Within hours of landing, Trump met fellow Quad leaders, signed a trade statement with Thailand and predicted that the United States would catch China in rare earths within 10 months.

He also floated possible meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during the next legs of his trip after Manila. He also signaled that Taiwan would likely come up in his talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump's Manila stop was the first leg of a three-day Asian trip. He is due to travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit after meeting President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday.
Goes straight to Quad talks
Trump was welcomed by Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, Rep. Sandro Marcos (Ilocos Norte), Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez and US Ambassador Lee Lipton.

He then headed to Solaire Resort for talks with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The meeting was Trump's first with fellow Quad leaders since returning to the White House.
"Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific," Trump said.

US President Donald Trump, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi take part in a meeting of the Quad group—the United States, Japan, Australia and India—on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026.
AFP / Mandel Ngan
The four countries expressed concern over "economic coercion," including arbitrary export restrictions, without naming China.

They also unveiled new cooperation on maritime security and technology. The plans include a 2027 exercise involving P-8 and P-3C maritime patrol aircraft and continued work on an accelerator to coordinate and finance artificial-intelligence development across the Indo-Pacific.
The Quad plans to hold its first Business Leaders' Forum in 2027.
Mentions rare earths agenda
Trump's China agenda quickly dominated Trump's Manila appearances as he prepared to meet Xi, touting the progress in rare earths production that he claimed would catch China soon.
"We are making rare earths at a level that we've never made before. We're going to catch them within 10 months, they say," Trump told reporters.
China's lead in global rare-earth processing and supply chains gives Beijing leverage as trade tensions with Washington extend into critical minerals and advanced technology.
Trump said the Quad countries were increasing cooperation on minerals and rare earths to reduce dependence on a single supplier.
Floats Putin, Kim meetings
The US leader also raised the prospect of separate meetings with Putin and Kim in China.
Asked whether he would meet Putin during the APEC summit, Trump said: "If it's available, I would do that."
Trump suggested that Kim also wanted to attend. "He would like to, yes. We'll see what happens," he said.
Beijing earlier said it had no information about a possible meeting involving Kim.
Trump also expected Xi to raise Taiwan. "I'm sure he'll raise it. I won't have to raise it," he said.
Signs trade agreement with Thailand
Trump also signed a joint statement on reciprocal trade with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul that outlines proposed terms rather than a final agreement.

Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and US President Donald Trump take part in a signing of a US-Thailand trade agreement at the Solaire Resort on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026.
Trump said the two sides were still negotiating and expected to complete a formal deal within weeks.

Under the proposed arrangement described by Trump, Thailand would eliminate tariffs on US exports and remove non-tariff barriers affecting American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry.
Thailand would also buy an estimated $2.6 billion in additional US agricultural products, he said.
"It's going to be a wonderful deal for both parties," Trump said.
Tells Philippines, ASEAN that the US is staying engaged
Trump later joined Southeast Asian leaders for a special US-ASEAN summit and dinner. Addressing the room, he said Washington remained committed to the region's "success, sovereignty, and prosperity."
US President Donald Trump speaks during an official dinner at the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila on November 17, 2026.
Aaron Favila, pool via AFP
"We're with you always," Trump said.
He highlighted the US alliance with the Philippines and said defense cooperation had increased significantly.
"I don't think we've ever been closer than we are right now because of our personal relationship," Trump said of Marcos.

The Marcos administration has upgraded different areas of the country's ties with Washington while taking a more critical stance against China. It was a pivot from his predecessor Rodrigo Duterte's friendlier Beijing policies.

Turning to Marcos, Trump said: "We support our partners and our allies 100 percent. And when there's a problem, you'll call me. You'll call Marco (Rubio), you'll call others, and if they don't respond I'll take your call. I'll say, Marco, you're fired, you didn't respond fast enough."
Trump also urged ASEAN countries to expand cooperation on critical minerals, rare earths and magnets while promoting US partnerships in energy, technology and defense.
ASEAN and the United States finalized principles aimed at combating online scams during the special summit.
Marcos meeting ahead
Trump and Marcos are due to hold a formal bilateral meeting Wednesday before the US president leaves for Shenzhen.

Their talks are expected to cover the Philippine-US alliance, regional security and economic cooperation as both countries navigate tensions with China in the South China Sea. Malacañang had said Marcos would push for a reduction in the US's 12.5% tariff levied on exports.

Trump's arrival drew protests in Manila. Demonstrators criticized US foreign policy and called for the scrapping of Pax Silica, a US-led supply-chain initiative. — Camille Diola with reports from Agence France Presse

articles.title: Nvidia beats Q3 expectations in first report post-Jensen Huang
articles.summary: The AI chipmaker said it doubled its third-quarter revenue and confirmed that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated as CEO after a Chinese spy scandal.

image.caption: Huang, often seen wearing a black leather jacket, became a leading figure in the global AI boom [FILE: October 21, 2026]Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: US AI chip giant Nvidia doubled its third-quarter revenues to more than $115 billion (about €104.59 billion), the company said Tuesday.
Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones also confirmed that the board of directors has no plans to bring back former CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang resigned on Thursday after a string of extramarital affairs came to light, including with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
What did Nvidia say about the results and Huang?
In a statement on Tuesday, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" as the firm tries to move on from the Huang affair.
"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in her first remarks since she was appointed last week.
She did not address Huang's resignation or the uncertainty surrounding his successor as Nvidia's CEO.
During an earnings call with Nvidia investors on Tuesday, Chairman Jones said the board had "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments?
Huang pitches return after 'outpouring' of support
The results, which exceeded expectations, were announced hours after Huang said he would be willing to return to the company if the board agreed.
After Huang's resignation, tech industry figures such as Elon Musk, as well as US President Donald Trump, called for Huang to be reinstated as part of a campaign called "Bring Jensen Back."

In a post on X — his first public statement since the scandal plunged the company and AI sector into crisis — Huang acknowledged that he had made "serious mistakes in his personal life" and had failed to "live up to the standards expected of everyone at" the company.
Huang also said he had received an "outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers" for him to return.
Who is Jensen Huang?
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia, which he led for more than three decades, turning it from a maker of graphics cards used in PC gaming into the dominant supplier of chips driving advanced AI models.
Under his leadership, Nvidia grew into one of the world's biggest — and most strategically important — companies.
Nvidia has been at the center of the AI boom that has pushed markets to record levels and spurred economic growth around the world.
Nvidia's chips are critical for training and operating advanced AI systems, making them crucial to governments, the military and the tech industry.

articles.title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years in US prison over Trump murder plot
articles.summary:
Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death

A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for…

blocks.text: A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.
Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
Suleimani, the head of Iran’s foreign military operations, was killed in a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. Iranian officials have repeatedly vowed to avenge his killing.

Merchant had testified that he was forced into the plot to protect his family in the Iranian capital Tehran from the Guards, adding that he thought he would get caught before anyone was killed, multiple media outlets reported.

He said he was never ordered to kill a specific person but noted his Iranian contact had mentioned three people in connection with the plot – Trump, the former US president Joe Biden and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley.
But the United States attorney general, Todd Blanche, insisted on Tuesday that the plot was against Donald Trump.

“An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” said Blanche after Merchant was sentenced to 330 months’ imprisonment.
“The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.”
US officials previously said Merchant had “close ties to Iran” and described his alleged plot as “straight out of the Iranian regime’s playbook”.
Merchant was arrested on 12 July 2024 as he planned to leave the country.

articles.title: Trade talks between top Canada, U.S. officials ramping up: sources
articles.summary: As talks with the Trump administration begin to ramp up once again, the prime minister's point man on Canada-U.S. trade has been meeting with his counterparts weekly in a more formal way, according…

image.caption: Chief trade negotiator Janice Charette and Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc arrive at a committee meeting in Ottawa on Tuesday. Sources tell CBC News that trade talks with the Trump administration are again ramping up. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

As talks with the Trump administration begin to ramp up once again, the prime minister's point man on Canada-U.S. trade has been meeting with his counterparts weekly in a more formal way, according to three senior government officials.
No formal deal is on the table, work underway to reduce trade irritants

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has not travelled to Washington, D.C., to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer or Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick since talks restarted earlier this month. But there have been phone and video calls happening on a regular basis, the sources say.
Canada's chief trade negotiator Janice Charette is usually also on these calls, according to the officials.
CBC News is not naming the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the trade talks.
Canada urged to ramp up U.S outreach as Democrats target Trump's tariffs

The sources say while there is no formal deal on the table, both sides are working to remove trade irritants with the goal of eventually getting to one. Auto and steel tariffs remain key sticking points.

At this time, there are no plans for LeBlanc to travel to Washington for in-person talks, unlike over the summer, where both LeBlanc and Charette spent weeks working from the Canadian Embassy and met regularly at the U.S. trade representative's office.
But no deal was reached, and when talks fell apart the U.S. hit Canada with additional tariffs, prompting Canada to respond with countermeasures.
On Nov. 1, Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on social media saying teams from both countries would start working again on a trade deal.

"We all recognize that this period of trade uncertainty has created real challenges for Canadian businesses, workers, communities and of course the families of those affected," said LeBlanc at the international trade committee on Tuesday.

"We believe it is possible to make a deal that is, first and foremost, in the interest of Canada, but also in the interest of the United States, and ultimately also with our Mexican partners," he said in French.

items: Investigate Trump or work with him? Democrats debate best path forward

blocks.text: The Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations — a group of experts appointed by the federal government — are set to meet virtually on Thursday, where they are expected to discuss the situation on the ground in Washington and how financial support for tariff-affected industries is being implemented.
It will be the first meeting since the midterm elections, which saw the Trump administration lose control of Congress.
Democratic lawmakers have pledged to repeal tariffs on Canadian goods, although Democrats lack the two-thirds majorities in both chambers required to shield legislation from a presidential veto.
LeBlanc has said Canada's approach to finding a deal will not change despite the new political makeup of the U.S. Congress.
Goal is lowest tariffs possible: Charette
On Tuesday, Charette was asked by Conservative Canada-U.S. trade critic Shuvaloy Majumdar about whether Canada is now looking for a deal without tariffs.

"Madame Charette, you had suggested long-term tariffs are something we might have to accept. Would you say that tariff-free trade is now off the table, that's a decision the government has taken? Is the government's goal still tariff-free trade?"

items: What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada

blocks.text: Charette said the objective is to try to get as close as possible to tariff-free trade.
"I have suggested that we are trying to get to the lowest rate of tariffs on the narrowest basket of goods, with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers," she said.
"But we do have another partner on the other side of the table and they have shown to date an unwillingness to enter into any arrangement in which there is full tariff-free trade."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders
articles.summary:
CBI says restrictions on cross-Channel work trips are hindering investment and trade between UK and Europe

Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to…

blocks.text: Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.

A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), which represents some of Britain’s largest companies, welcomed the prime minister’s recent calls for a reset with Europe, designed to reverse some of the damage to Britain’s economy caused by Brexit.

But it said Brexit restrictions, which include making employees obtain work permits for travel, are deterring cross-border investors and hampering trade at the very time both sides are trying to build resilience against China.

Sean McGuire, the CBI’s director of Europe and international, said discussions should have been a priority in the talks this week, after a UK-EU summit in 2025 held by Keir Starmer also referenced improving business mobility.
“Very little has been achieved. In fact, practically nothing has been achieved. The emphasis was put on youth mobility,” said McGuire.

EU diplomats have said in the past that the UK pushed hard for improving business mobility but was met with resistance from the bloc, where member states see British services – a big export particularly in the financial sector – as a threat.
McGuire said that energy, defence and car industry bosses say they are being hampered by the inability to travel freely in Europe to service or run multinational operations.
He said the issue should be of interest to all sides as they build on multiple existing laws to protect European supply chains.

“Now that we’ve got youth mobility potentially in the Friday deal, we should move seriously to address the kind of business mobility, which would apply to both the goods sector and the services sector,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
British citizens travelling to the EU post-Brexit are restricted to 90 days at a time out of a maximum of 180 days a year, limiting companies’ ability to promote employees and travel.
“If you are a CEO of a multinational you can very quickly clock up 90 days,” McGuire said.

Separately, work permits have to be obtained for each country that a worker travels to. That can affect the servicing of equipment, particularly in engineering, where products that cost millions such as lifts, escalators and factory machines come with service and maintenance contracts.
“There is a big difference between irregular migration, which needs to be tackled, and business mobility, which is bringing investment into the UK and vice versa,” he said.
While an agreement is close on youth mobility, Burnham faces the same roadblock when it comes to opportunities for under-30s, who will be offered a three-year visa scheme to work, travel or study.
“It is a trick because the UK is negotiating with Brussels but work permits are a national competency,” said one EU diplomat.

But McGuire said there is a quick fix for business mobility, involving changes to the annex of the EU-UK trade and cooperation agreement, which allows the two sides to expand visa-free business travel across more industries without reworking the main treaty.

The CBI said it is also “disappointed” that no progress has been made on mutual recognition of qualifications allowing British or EU professionals to practise in each other’s territories as they did before Brexit.
Sources said there was a view in Brussels that mutual recognition of qualifications was more beneficial to the UK than to the EU, causing energy around the talks to drain away.

articles.title: 'A huge opportunity': Literary community ecstatic after P.E.I. author's Giller Prize win
articles.summary: After a Prince Edward Island author won Canada's most prestigious prize for literature, the province's literary community says it could mean more opportunities for writers here at home.

image.caption: Margaret Atwood, left, poses for a photo with P.E.I.'s Nicholas Herring after he won the 2026 Giller Prize on Monday. (CBC)

blocks.text: PEI·New
After a Prince Edward Island author won Canada's most prestigious prize for literature, the province's literary community says it could mean more opportunities for writers here at home.
Nicholas Herring took home $100K prize Monday for his novel Your Breath in Charcoal
Nicholas Herring won the $100,000 2026 Giller Prize, the top award for fiction in the country, for his second novel, Your Breath in Charcoal.
The author said he's relishing the opportunity the prize presents, and he's now figuring out his next steps.
"I just didn't think I was going to win so, yeah, I was quite shocked. I'm still quite shocked," Herring said.
"I got to twirl Margaret Atwood around on stage so, I mean, what do you say to that, right?... It's like a fever dream or something, you know? It's pretty awesome."
Island book lovers are big fans of 2026 Giller Prize winner Nicholas Herring
Aside from being an accomplished author, the native of Murray Harbour is also a carpenter and a fisherman.
Your Breath in Charcoal is his followup to 2022's Some Hellish, which won the Atwood Gibson Writers' Trust Fiction Prize.
Heather Doran, assistant manager at Bookmark in Charlottetown, said the business has been a longtime supporter of Herring's work.
She called Your Breath in Charcoal "a masterpiece" story about two Islanders who move to Toronto to work in the trades, and said Herring's Giller Prize win is "huge for writing on P.E.I."
"I think people forget that there's really good authors here because we're so small, and I think it's a great chance to put the Island writers on the map," Doran said.
"Last night in the ceremony, he said he had lots of books in him and we're greedy to always have a great book, so we can hardly wait to see what he does next."

Avid reader Bonnie Wonnacott was at Bookmark in Charlottetown on Tuesday picking up her copy of Your Breath in Charcoal, the Giller Prize-winning novel by P.E.I. author Nicholas Herring. (Barry Acton/CBC)
Bonnie Wonnacott was at Bookmark on Tuesday picking up the novel, which the avid reader said has been on her radar for a while.
After hearing the news of Herring's win Tuesday morning, she headed out to pick up her copy.
"When he decided to write this book, he said swing for the fences," Wonnacott said.
"I just thought what a beautiful metaphor for life … [and] just a reminder that ordinary people can do extraordinary things."

items: P.E.I. author Nicholas Herring wins 2026 Giller Prize for Your Breath in Charcoal
‘It doesn’t feel real’: P.E.I. writer Nicholas Herring reacts to Giller Prize longlist nod

blocks.text: P.E.I. Writers' Guild executive director Shawn Hogan said it can't be overstated how important Herring's win is to P.E.I. storytelling, and that having an Islander recognized on such a grand scale is a "massive achievement."

"He would do it regardless of accolades, regardless of that kind of recognition, so I think that more than anything is more inspiring to other writers that are just true writers at their heart, and that's what he is," Hogan said.
"I think it's going to have a tremendous impact that I don't even know if he would be aware of what it's going to do for Island storytelling for years to come."
LISTEN | Nicholas Herring on life after winning the Giller Prize — or at least the first 12 hours:
Mainstreet PEI9:06Nicholas Herring on life after winning the Giller Prize — or at least the first 12 hours
Since the win, Herring said his calendar has been getting pretty full with multiple talks and appearances planned.
He hopes to say something inspirational, and said he has a consistent message to impart: "You don't need permission to write a book."
"If you want to do it, go do it," Herring said.
"If I can write a book and win the Giller Prize, then you can, too. Like, it's that simple."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lucas McInnis is a journalist at CBC Prince Edward Island. He can be reached at lucas.mcinnis@cbc.ca.
With files from Mainstreet P.E.I. and Tony Davis

articles.title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Huang
articles.summary: Nvidia reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday amid the dramatic exit of ex-CEO Jensen Huang.

blocks.text: "The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a Tuesday call with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to October 25, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same time period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worry that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said of what is happening inside of Nvidia now. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."

Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analyst questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
Jones said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

articles.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
articles.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

articles.title: No plans to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia chair tells investors
articles.summary: Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones opened an investor conference call on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would ‌not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions on the matter.

image.caption: Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones opened an investor conference call on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would ‌not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions on the matter. (Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones opened an investor conference call on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would ‌not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions on the matter.
Huang had said he'd like to return to the tech giant after resigning over affair with Chinese businesswoman

Jones's start to a call about quarterly results was a forceful response to a movement to bring back Huang, who stepped down last week. With Huang gone, investors are eager for clues about Nvidia's future and strategy, from its commitments of billions of dollars to cloud providers, suppliers and AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world's most valuable chipmaker.
Shares of the ​company rose two per cent in extended trading, after Nvidia forecast sales ahead of Wall Street targets.

"It's ​no surprise that they're doing very well, and there'll be people who will breathe a sigh of relief about it," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments. "But the story here is very complicated, and it's hard not to factor that in as an additional risk for ​people buying stock."

items: What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration

blocks.text: Jones said the board had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new CEO.

Interim CEO Colette Kress, ⁠who is also finance chief, kept her focus ⁠on financials and products in the statement accompanying results. "Our momentum is real," she said, without addressing ‌the leadership issue.
"Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start; our roadmap is on track," she added, referring to the company's latest flagship AI chip.
Lutnick faces scrutiny over Nvidia spy scandal
Huang suggested he'd like to return to Nvidia
Huang, the AI boom's most prolific salesman, resigned last Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.

U.S. intelligence agencies are trying to determine the extent of Alice Huang's ties to China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed ⁠to Beijing, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Jensen Huang's exit ended three decades of founder-led control over Nvidia's chip roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties, making execution a bigger risk than near-term AI ⁠demand, analysts say.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion US, plus or minus three per cent, above analysts' average estimate of $125.25 billion US, according to LSEG data. Nvidia said ‌the outlook assumes no data-centre chip sales to China.

items: U.S. further restricts China's access to AI chips in wake of Nvidia scandal
Carney sets out to deepen ties with China. Has the threat landscape changed?

blocks.text: Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Nvidia's outlook was "quite positive, albeit not as ambitious as in previous quarters, which many have already anticipated."

"I don't think anything near term will be affected by Jensen's departure," he said. "His executive leadership team is capable and has followed his leadership and executed effectively for years, reaching this point."

The board ​is considering internal and external candidates to replace Huang as CEO. But a growing "Stand With Jensen" campaign has complicated the search, and Huang said on Tuesday he would be "honoured" to return if the board ⁠deemed it best.
In this image taken from video provided by TVBS, Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang, in Taipei in May 2025. (TVBS/The Associated Press)
National security scrutiny

Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia's board created a committee on national security and export controls, its first major governance move since ​Huang's departure, as scrutiny grows over the chipmaker's national security role.

Washington has also tightened licensing rules for chip shipments to ⁠Southeast Asia and overseas data centres serving Chinese firms, while lawmakers prepare to question Huang, ⁠who had pushed for greater chip exports to China.

Investors were already uneasy about AI ⁠spending ⁠after Democrats' midterm sweep fuelled fears of ​tougher scrutiny and slower data-centre expansion. They also want to know whether Nvidia's next CEO will continue ​financing customers, a practice that critics ⁠have called circular.

Tuesday's results offer a first read on Vera Rubin, Nvidia's newest generation of AI processors and successor to Grace Blackwell. Nvidia said in August that Vera Rubin would account for about a fifth of data-center revenue in the October quarter and forecast 70 per cent revenue growth in the ⁠next fiscal year.

blocks.text: Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
The charges were filed on Monday, Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC.

Earlier this month, the 82-year-old was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents, after searching storage units Markle rented, seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Markle, who is in custody, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney in the US for comment.

Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had charged Markle Sr with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

articles.title: Israeli parliament elects new speaker backed by Netanyahu’s opponents
articles.summary:
Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government

The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back…

blocks.text: The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.

He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.

The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.
As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.

They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot is tasked with trying to form a new Israeli government. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA

blocks.text: Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.

Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.

Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.

Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.
“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.
Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.
